comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to submit my formal comment in strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to implement a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for STEM OPT extensions. While the stated intent of this rule is to protect domestic workers and prevent program reliance, an empirical, data-driven analysis of the international student ecosystem demonstrates that this astronomical fee structure will severely damage U.S. higher education, stifle critical talent pipelines, and cause net harm to local and national economies.

1. The Financial Stabilization of U.S. Higher Education
International students act as a critical financial pillar for American universities. The vast majority of international undergraduates and master's students pay full, out-of-state tuition entirely out-of-pocket, with virtually no access to federal financial aid or state subsidies. According to data from NAFSA: Association of International Educators, during the 2022-2023 academic year alone, international students contributed $40.1 billion to the U.S. economy and supported over 368,000 jobs. This massive influx of out-of-state tuition directly subsidizes institutional infrastructure, research facilities, and financial aid budgets that make higher education more affordable for domestic, in-state American students. Imposing a massive financial barrier at the post-completion stage will cause a sharp decline in international enrollment, leaving universities with severe budget shortfalls.

2. Direct Contributions to Local Businesses and Consumer Markets
International students do not live in an economic vacuum. During their years of study and subsequent operational training, they spend billions of dollars directly supporting local economies. This includes housing rentals, grocery stores, automotive purchases, utilities, consumer electronics, and local services. By discouraging international students from choosing the United States, DHS is effectively draining consumer capital out of college towns and metropolitan areas across the country, directly harming small businesses that rely on student populations to sustain their operations.

3. Fiscal Contributions Through Taxation and Work-Authorized Spending
When international graduates transition to OPT and STEM OPT, they become highly productive, tax-paying contributors to the U.S. labor force. Individuals working on OPT are subject to federal, state, and local income taxes. The wages earned by these specialized professionals are immediately recycled back into the U.S. economy through local rent, consumer spending, and tax revenues, creating a robust fiscal multiplier effect. A $70,000 baseline fee transforms the OPT program from an earned opportunity into an unviable financial liability, cutting off these vital tax streams.

4. Destruction of Critical STEM and Technology Talent Pipelines
The United States is currently facing severe domestic skill shortages in highly specialized technical fields, including critical infrastructure areas such as Mainframe systems, software engineering, and Artificial Intelligence (AI). American corporations rely on the OPT and STEM OPT programs to bridge these operational gaps with U.S.-educated talent. Forcing universities or employers to absorb a combined $100,000 in regulatory fees to authorize a single graduate completely blocks the entry-level talent pipeline. Instead of protecting domestic jobs, this policy will compel multinational corporations to outsource critical technology operations, engineering hubs, and high-value projects overseas to countries with more competitive talent pipelines, such as India, China, Canada, the United Kingdom, or Australia.

Conclusion
The proposed fee structure is economically prohibitive and legally counterproductive. It fails to account for the profound economic benefits that international students provide through out-of-state tuition, local consumer spending, and critical technical labor. I strongly urge the Department to withdraw this proposal and maintain the standard, accessible infrastructure of the OPT program to ensure the United States remains the global leader in innovation and economic growth.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they will harm the U.S. economy and higher education.

Housing is already too expensive in many American communities. We should be looking for ways to build homes more efficiently, not overlooking policies that could make construction workforce development more difficult.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 (RIN 1653-AB01), Comment in Opposition to the Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for each subsequent OPT recommendation. I am an F-1 master's student in Computer Science. I moved across the world to pursue this degree, and this rule would change the terms of that decision after I have already made it. I urge DHS to withdraw it.

1. The fee would effectively eliminate OPT for most students.
This is not a nominal administrative charge. It is more than a year of tuition and living costs for many international students, and it applies to every student seeking OPT. Schools must pay it before a DSO can enter an OPT recommendation, and it is not refundable once an EAD is issued. DHS acknowledges schools may pass the cost on to students. Very few schools can absorb $70,000 per student, so students must pay it themselves or lose OPT. Most cannot, having already spent their savings or taken on debt for their degrees.

2. Current students are being punished for decisions made under different rules.
I and thousands of other students enrolled in good faith under the rules as they stood. We paid application, SEVIS, and visa fees, tuition, relocation costs, and a year or more of living expenses, tens of thousands of dollars in total, understanding that OPT was part of the path. DHS says applying the rule only to recommendations dated after the effective date addresses reliance interests. It does not. A student who has not yet received a recommendation has already spent the money and moved their life. DHS itself concedes in a footnote that current students are in a different position, then dismisses their reliance anyway. At minimum, every student enrolled before this proposal was published on October 8, 2026 should be fully exempt.

3. The timing makes the harm worse.
Technology graduates face one of the hardest entry-level job markets in years, and DHS's own proposal cites high unemployment among recent computer science graduates. A $70,000 charge attached to the work authorization we need to get that first job makes us less hireable. Many employers will simply skip us. The rule would close the main door through which international graduates, who have invested heavily in U.S. education, can start their careers.

4. The rule will drive away future students and hurt U.S. universities.
DHS notes that only about 20 percent of F-1 students used OPT in 2024 and treats OPT as incidental to the decision to study here. That reasoning is flawed. OPT use is concentrated among graduate students in STEM and other high-demand fields, the students U.S. universities and employers most want. For them, practical training is a central reason to choose the United States over Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, or Germany. DHS's own regulatory analysis recognizes that institutions could see enrollment declines and lost tuition revenue, yet says these cannot be precisely quantified. Prospective students will see a six-figure penalty on top of tuition and choose another country. Universities, local economies, research programs, and employers would all bear the cost.

5. The fraud concerns do not justify a fee this broad.
Fraud by shell companies and visa mills deserves enforcement. But a blanket fee punishes the honest majority, treating students at reputable universities with legitimate employers the same as the schemes DHS describes. DHS rejected targeted alternatives such as expanded site visits, reporting, and stricter procedures in a single paragraph. Those would address fraud directly without destroying legitimate OPT.

6. I oppose charging the initial fee again at each degree level.
This alternative, on which DHS invites comment, would make it nearly impossible to pursue advanced degrees in the United States.

Requests: I respectfully ask that DHS (1) withdraw the proposed rule; (2) if not withdrawn, exempt all students enrolled on or before October 8, 2026, including post-completion and STEM OPT; (3) sharply reduce the fee and tie it to demonstrated risk, such as schools or employers with documented compliance problems; (4) reject the per-degree-level alternative; and (5) publish a full analysis of the effect on international enrollment and university revenue before any final rule.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they are prohibitive and unfairly punish current students.

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I respectfully request that the Department reconsider the proposed fees associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT).

International students come to the United States legally, follow immigration regulations, and invest significant amounts of money in their education. Many students and their families make considerable financial sacrifices because they believe in the quality of American education and the opportunities it provides.

OPT is an important part of that educational experience. It allows students to apply what they have learned in the classroom, gain practical experience, and contribute their knowledge and skills to American businesses and the economy.

I understand that the government has a responsibility to maintain immigration oversight and ensure that programs operate effectively. However, I am concerned that the proposed fees are disproportionately high and could create serious financial and administrative burdens for universities and students.

Even if these fees are initially charged to educational institutions, the costs could ultimately affect students through higher tuition, additional charges, or reduced access to OPT opportunities.

I also believe this proposal could have unintended consequences for the United States. International students contribute to universities, local communities, research, and the workforce. Making practical training significantly more expensive could discourage talented students from choosing American universities and make it harder for employers to benefit from their skills.

I respectfully encourage the Department to consider less burdensome alternatives, including fees that are proportionate to actual administrative costs, and to carefully evaluate the economic and educational consequences before finalizing this proposal.

I support reasonable immigration regulations and appropriate oversight. My concern is simply that students who have followed the legal process and invested in an American education should have a fair opportunity to gain practical experience without facing unnecessary financial barriers.

Thank you for considering this comment and for allowing the public to participate in the rulemaking process.

Respectfully,

An International Student

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my concerns about DHS's proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations under 8 CFR 214.13.

While I recognize the government's responsibility to prevent immigration fraud and protect American workers, the proposed fee structure could create significant unintended economic consequences for American businesses, universities, and the broader U.S. economy.

1. Negative Impact on American Businesses and Workforce Development

OPT provides American employers with access to graduates who have received education and training in the United States. Many of these individuals develop specialized skills, gain familiarity with American industries, and are prepared to contribute immediately to the workforce.

If schools become unwilling or unable to pay the proposed fees, businesses could lose access to qualified candidates who are already educated and available in the United States. Recruiting replacements takes time and money, and suitable domestic candidates may not always be readily available for specialized positions.

This could increase hiring costs, delay projects, reduce productivity, and make it more difficult for American businesses, particularly small and medium-sized companies, to compete and innovate.

Restricting access to OPT does not automatically create an equivalent supply of qualified American workers. It could instead leave businesses with fewer qualified candidates and greater operational challenges.

2. Negative Impact on American Universities and the Education Sector

International students contribute significantly to American universities through tuition, research, academic collaboration, and innovation.

The availability of practical training opportunities is also an important consideration for many students choosing where to pursue higher education.

If universities face a $70,000 financial obligation for each initial OPT recommendation, they may become reluctant to support otherwise qualified students. This could discourage prospective international students from choosing American institutions, reducing university enrollment and revenue.

Over time, the United States could lose not only international tuition revenue but also valuable research talent and the economic contributions associated with international education.

3. The Proposed Fees Are Not a Targeted Approach to Preventing Fraud

I understand DHS's concerns about fraudulent OPT employment and abuse of the program. However, imposing the same extraordinary fee on every student does not distinguish between legitimate employment and fraudulent activity.

A student with a genuine job offer from a reputable American company should not face the same financial barrier as someone involved in a fraudulent arrangement.

DHS should prioritize targeted audits of high-risk institutions, investigations of fraudulent employers, and stronger verification of actual employment and training activities.

These measures would address the underlying problems more directly without unnecessarily restricting legitimate employment opportunities or imposing disproportionate costs on compliant universities and businesses.

4. The Economic Costs Deserve Greater Consideration

DHS's own regulatory analysis acknowledges that reduced OPT participation could result in productivity losses for employers, lower international student enrollment, and lost economic opportunities.

It also estimates annual fee collections ranging from $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion. However, the analysis acknowledges that there is insufficient data to precisely quantify the broader economic value lost when students cannot participate in OPT.

Government revenue should not be treated as an adequate measure of economic benefit. The long-term contributions of skilled workers, productive businesses, university research, and innovation must also be considered.

A policy that generates substantial fee revenue while reducing access to qualified talent may ultimately impose costs on the American economy that outweigh its intended benefits.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure.

If the objective is to strengthen OPT program integrity and protect American workers, DHS should pursue targeted enforcement, improved oversight, and risk-based compliance measures rather than imposing extraordinary financial barriers on every OPT recommendation.

The United States benefits when its universities educate talented individuals and its businesses have the opportunity to employ qualified graduates. OPT serves as an important connection between American higher education and the domestic workforce.

Protecting program integrity and maintaining America's ability to attract talent should be complementary goals, not competing ones.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees will negatively impact American businesses, universities, and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 (RIN 1653-AB01), Comment in Opposition to the Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees. I am an F-1 master's student in Computer Science. I moved across the world to pursue this degree, and this rule would change the terms of that decision after I have made it. The rule contradicts its own rationale in several ways. I urge DHS to withdraw it.

1. The fee cannot fund the oversight DHS says it needs. DHS says it cannot operate OPT consistent with its focus on fraud without the fees. Yet the rule states the fees would be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, that ICE would not keep or use them, and that they are not earmarked for SEVP or enforcement. The fee raises no resources for oversight. DHS also designs the rule to shrink OPT, expecting a smaller pool of participants and treating unpaid fees as lost participation. A fee that succeeds by deterring use produces less revenue, and a fee that produces revenue has failed to deter. DHS does not say which it expects.

2. The remedy does not match the fraud described. DHS's examples involve shell employers, fake worksites, and visa mills, such as 15 students arrested in 2020. DHS's largest figure, more than 10,000 students working for highly suspect employers, is about 5 percent of the 194,554 students who received OPT in 2024, and those cases are suspected, not confirmed. The fee is paid by schools and, in practice, students. Employers pay nothing, even though DHS's worker-protection concerns, including wages and the FICA exemption, are employer-side. The rule does not address FICA. It also states it does not address CPT. A blanket fee on every honest student is not tailored to the conduct DHS describes.

3. DHS points students to the H-1B while pricing that path out. The rule says F-1 students may pursue employment through the H-1B, yet sets the OPT fee to align with H-1B fees and cites the $100,000 H-1B proclamation. Raising both fees leaves international graduates with no workable route to employment.

4. The rule creates the foreign-funding risk it warns about. DHS says large foreign payments toward OPT fees could be red flags for adversaries seeking to subsidize schools. But it sets six-figure per-student costs, allows schools to pass them to students, and imposes no limits on how fees are funded. That increases the incentive for outside funding.

5. Pre-completion OPT is penalized. DHS's own example has a school paying $70,000 for a student's pre-completion OPT and $30,000 for post-completion OPT with the same employer, $100,000 in total. That discourages the hands-on training directly related to a student's major that DHS says OPT exists to provide. Refunds are discretionary and not appealable.

6. Current students bear costs they could not foresee. We enrolled in good faith, paying application, SEVIS, and visa fees, tuition, relocation, and living costs, tens of thousands of dollars in total, understanding OPT was part of the path. DHS applies the rule to any recommendation dated after the effective date and admits current students are differently situated than prospective ones, then dismisses their reliance. At minimum, all students enrolled before October 8, 2026 should be exempt.

7. The harms are acknowledged but not measured. DHS concedes enrollment declines and lost tuition revenue are possible but cannot quantify them. It rejected exempting small schools because 56 percent are small entities, while admitting it cannot predict how many would be affected. It dismisses OPT's role in enrollment by noting only 20 percent of F-1 students used it in 2024, ignoring that use is concentrated among STEM graduate students. In a weak entry-level technology job market, the fee makes international graduates harder to hire, and prospective students will study in Canada, the United Kingdom, or Australia instead.

8. I oppose charging the initial fee again at each degree level, which would make advanced degrees nearly impossible.

I respectfully ask that DHS (1) withdraw the rule; (2) if not, exempt students enrolled before October 8, 2026, including STEM OPT; (3) replace the blanket fee with targeted measures against documented bad actors; (4) reject the per-degree alternative; and (5) publish expected participation, revenue, and enrollment estimates before any final rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject: Protecting America’s Global Competitiveness by Retaining International Talent

The United States has long been a global leader in innovation, technology, and economic growth because of its ability to attract and retain talented individuals from around the world. International students and skilled foreign professionals contribute not only their technical expertise, but also diverse perspectives, new ideas, and entrepreneurial ambition that strengthen American industries.

Optional Practical Training (OPT) plays a critical role in connecting highly educated international graduates with the American workforce. It allows U.S. companies to benefit from talent trained at American universities, particularly in high-demand fields such as artificial intelligence, software engineering, and advanced technology.

Imposing additional financial burdens or restricting employment opportunities for international graduates would risk driving highly skilled talent to competing countries. After investing years in educating these individuals, the United States should not create unnecessary barriers that prevent American companies from benefiting from their knowledge and skills.

Such restrictions could ultimately slow technological innovation, weaken American businesses, discourage international talent from choosing American universities, and undermine the nation’s long-term economic competitiveness.

Countries around the world are competing to attract the brightest minds. If the United States makes it increasingly difficult for talented graduates to contribute to its economy, other nations will gladly welcome them.

America’s greatest strength has always been its ability to attract talent, foster innovation, and turn ideas into progress. Protecting that advantage is not simply about supporting international students. It is about protecting America’s economic future.

I strongly encourage policymakers to consider these long-term consequences and preserve accessible pathways for highly skilled international graduates to contribute to the American workforce.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that additional financial burdens and restrictions on OPT will harm American competitiveness and workforce.

comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern:

I respectfully request reconsideration of the proposed rule that would impose a $70,000 fee on educational institutions seeking to recommend students for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for STEM OPT recommendations.

The F-1 student program allows international students, who have lawfully entered the United States after a rigorous screening and admission process, to pursue higher education and contribute to our academic institutions. Upon completion of their degree programs, OPT and STEM OPT provide these students with the opportunity to apply the knowledge and skills they have gained through authorized employment, benefiting both the students and the U.S. workforce.

International students make substantial contributions to our nation. They bring diverse perspectives, advanced knowledge, and exposure to emerging technologies and global innovations. In addition, they contribute significantly to the U.S. economy. Among all student populations, international students often pay the highest tuition rates, frequently paying two to three times more than in-state students. Beyond tuition, they support local economies through expenditures on housing, transportation, health insurance, food, and other goods and services.

Implementing fees of this magnitude would create an enormous financial burden on educational institutions and could discourage schools from participating in the OPT and STEM OPT programs. Such a policy could reduce educational opportunities for international students, decrease enrollment, and negatively affect universities, colleges, and local communities that depend on the economic activity generated by these students. In some cases, institutions could face financial hardship, resulting in job losses and reduced services, ultimately impacting U.S. workers and communities.

Furthermore, limiting opportunities for talented international graduates could weaken our nation's ability to remain competitive in a global economy. Other countries actively attract international students and highly skilled graduates by providing pathways for practical training and workforce participation. The United States should continue to welcome individuals who come here legally, invest heavily in their education, and contribute to our economy and workforce.

I fully support efforts to maintain the integrity of our immigration system and address unlawful activity. However, imposing excessively burdensome fees on institutions and students who are complying with the law and contributing positively to our society may have unintended and far-reaching consequences. Such measures could harm educational institutions, local economies, employers, and the nation's global competitiveness.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge USCIS and the appropriate authorities to reconsider this proposed regulation and carefully evaluate its potential economic and educational impact.

Thank you for your time, consideration, and commitment to policies that strengthen both our education system and our nation's future.

Sincerely,
MF
comments.reason: Argues the proposed OPT fees create an enormous financial burden and harm institutions and students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Drew Theological School (at Drew University)
comments.commentText:
PUBLIC COMMENT SUBMISSION
Agency: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) / U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)
Docket ID: ICEB-2026-0100-0001
Submitting Institution: Drew Theological School (Madison, New Jersey)

Drew Theological School is one of 13 United Methodist seminaries in the U.S. and is embedded in Drew University in Madison, New Jersey. We submit these comments to express strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule that would impose fees exceeding $70,000 on institutions filing for Optional Practical Training (OPT) per international student.

International students are a vital part of Drew University’s vibrant academic and civic community. In the Theological School, specifically, international students make up nearly 38% of Drew’s graduate student population. This Fall, almost half of our incoming Master of Divinity (MDiv) students are international students. These MDiv students choose Drew Theological School to earn a required professional degree to pursue their calling to serve as ordained religious leaders in churches and service organizations. This proposed rule threatens to severely damage student enrollment, financial stability, and global engagement.

In theological education, professional development and vocational formation extend beyond the classroom. Many of the academic programs offered in the Theological School require supervised internships for our students to engage in experiential learning. Optional Practical Training provides an indispensable extension of this mission, enabling students who bring gifts and expertise from a range of perspectives to apply their academic training in real-world U.S. environments. International students and graduates contribute to the vitality of congregations and the well-being of communities, including rural and underserved areas where qualified pastoral leadership can be difficult to secure. The proposed fee structure would dismantle this pathway and weaken our regional and national pool of qualified religious professionals.

Drew Theological School urges DHS not to adopt the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee or the $30,000 subsequent fee. The proposed fee introduces an unsustainable financial barrier, particularly for theological education, and passing a $70,000+ fee onto universities or the church judicatories who hope to engage our students will severely disrupt our partnerships. The costs are disproportionate to the financial capacity of many seminaries and churches and threatens legitimate educational and community-serving opportunities. The proposed fee would most certainly have a detrimental impact on small educational institutions, ministry employers, and underserved communities.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed rule imposing high OPT fees, stating it harms international students and enrollment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Gaurav chavan
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an F-1 student studying Engineering at Drexel University. I am writing to oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT.

OPT is a core part of my F-1 program's practical training. I came to the United States to study engineering, paying a lot in tuition and living costs, far from home, with very limited options to work while I study. OPT is the main chance I have to get the industry experience I need as an engineer. I have paid a lot for my education, and it is only fair that I have the chance to apply what I have learned in a real workplace. Without OPT, that investment and years of study would not lead to the practical experience employers expect.

A $70,000 fee, charged to my school before it can recommend OPT, would make OPT effectively unavailable to students like me. Schools cannot reasonably absorb that cost for every student, and many would have to limit or stop OPT recommendations. That would leave F-1 graduates without the practical training their programs were designed to include, and leave U.S. employers without a lawful, short-term way to hire them.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposal. If a fee is needed, it should be proportionate to the cost of administering OPT, not set at a level that ends the program in practice.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly support DHS's proposed OPT fee rule. OPT should serve its original educational purpose, not become a source of artificially inexpensive labor that disadvantages American graduates.

#1. Protecting Employment Opportunities for American Graduates
American graduates face increasingly difficult employment prospects. A striking example recently reported by *The Wall Street Journal* is Jack Weis, a 2024 Princeton University Ph.D. graduate in Chemical Engineering. He reportedly submitted more than 2,300 job applications over approximately two years without securing stable employment, despite his exceptional academic qualifications.

If even a Princeton Ph.D. graduate struggles to find work, the employment challenges facing ordinary American graduates deserve serious attention.

OPT should provide temporary practical training, not create an alternative labor supply that undermines American workers' opportunities.

# 2. Preventing Exploitative Employment Conditions
OPT can create employment arrangements resembling concerns raised about the H-1B system, including conditions described by Vice President JD Vance as resembling "indentured labor."

Some OPT workers may face:
- Lower compensation than similarly qualified American employees.
- Limited bargaining power because of immigration-related employment constraints.
- Reduced freedom to change employers or negotiate better conditions.
- Long-term compensation disadvantages that benefit employers.

The issue is not international graduates themselves, but the potential exploitation of their immigration status.

# 3. Preserving Appropriate Immigration Pathways
The United States should continue attracting exceptional international talent. However, existing pathways, including the O-1 visa for individuals with extraordinary ability, provide mechanisms for recruiting highly accomplished professionals.

Attracting exceptional talent should not require an expansive OPT system that disadvantages American entry-level graduates.

# 4. Preventing Unfair Employer Advantages
Employers should not be allowed to turn an educational training program into a source of artificially inexpensive labor.

When OPT workers receive lower compensation or have weaker bargaining power, employers may gain advantages over businesses that hire American graduates under normal labor market conditions.

The proposed fee structure can help discourage excessive reliance on OPT and reduce these competitive distortions.

# 5. Protecting the Public Interest
Universities have financial incentives to recruit international students because international tuition contributes substantially to institutional revenue. Post-graduation employment opportunities can also make their programs more attractive.

However, university financial interests should not override the interests of American workers. DHS should evaluate OPT based on its effects on domestic employment, immigration integrity, and the national interest.

# 6. Conclusion
The United States should welcome international students and exceptional global talent while protecting fair employment opportunities for American graduates.

OPT should remain an educational training program, not become a mechanism for providing employers with a structurally disadvantaged labor force.

I strongly support the proposed DHS rule as a measure to discourage misuse of OPT, reduce unfair labor cost advantages, and protect American employment opportunities.

American immigration policy should serve the national interest, protect fair competition, and ensure that American graduates have a reasonable opportunity to compete for jobs in their own country.**

Respectfully submitted,
A Concerned American Parent
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states support for the proposed OPT fee rule to protect American graduates and curb cheap labor.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Manuel Reis

I am writing as an international Master’s student in Artificial Intelligence (AI) to express strong concerns regarding the proposed increase in Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees.

Artificial Intelligence is a key driver of modern technological advancement and economic competitiveness in the United States. International students in STEM fields—particularly in advanced areas like AI, machine learning, and data science—contribute significantly to U.S. university research, innovation, and industry growth during their academic programs and through post-graduation training on OPT and STEM OPT extensions.

While I understand the agency's need to recover administrative costs, imposing higher financial burdens on international graduates creates several unintended consequences:

Increased Financial Strain on Early-Career Talent: International students already face substantial financial commitments, including high international tuition, mandatory fees, and strict limits on off-campus employment during their studies. Adding significant fee hikes at the transition into early-career practical training increases financial hardship precisely when students are transitioning between academics and professional roles.

Impact on American Technological Leadership: High financial barriers may disincentivize top global talent from choosing the United States for advanced degree programs in critical fields like AI. If foreign graduates face cost-prohibitive administrative processes, competing global tech hubs become more attractive, potentially weakening the U.S. pipeline of specialized AI talent.

Barriers for Startups and Emerging Research: OPT allows AI graduates to contribute to high-growth startups, research labs, and small enterprises that may not have the resources to sponsor immediate H-1B visas. Exorbitant entry fees restrict early-career innovation where it is needed most.

I respectfully request that the Immigration and Customs Enforcement Bureau reconsider the fee increase or implement a tiered/graduated fee structure that accounts for student status and non-profit/academic sector employment. Maintaining accessible, reasonable fee structures for OPT is vital for retaining world-class talent in critical STEM fields.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule.

comments.commentText:
I am a US citizen who completed a PhD in a STEM field in the US. I am currently a post-doctoral researcher in the US. I think this fee is exorbitant, unnecessary, ineffective for the stated purpose and will waste time, money and talent which could be put towards scientific breakthroughs.
I am commenting on the proposed rule change which would change the current filing fee from roughly $500 to an exorbitant $70,000 fee for initial OPT; and $30,000 fee for any subsequent Optional Practical Training (OPT) to “combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers.”
The time the visa process already takes seems more than sufficient for the task of preventing fraud already. My peers who are not from the US talk about the great amount of time and expense to get to an embassy in their country to go through the interview process to secure a visa. They have said the process was done with great care to verify who they are and their purpose in the US. I have never seen an instance of visa fraud in the entirety of my bachelors, masters, doctoral or post-doctoral training in academia.
Next, the proposed fee for this process is grossly exorbitant. To put it in perspective, I make $55,000 a year at an R1 institution, a PhD or graduate student working in a lab costs roughly $30,000. The professor I work for funds their lab through federal grants. If I were an international student, there is no way I could pay the proposed $70,000 fee myself with my salary and it would be a waste of taxpayer money to pass that cost on to my boss or the university. The cost of just the proposed fee could fund a postdoctoral researcher and a graduate student for a year. This is extreme and not feasible for labs which already make every dollar of grant money stretch to fund the necessary equipment and consumables for daily work in the lab.
Finally, this proposed rule wastes talent. Jobs in academia are extremely specialized. When a job is posted, there is an extremely limited number of people in the US and the world qualified to do that job. As I stated above, this fee would prevent international candidates from being considered for hiring in the first place. This would limit the candidate pool and may result in no suitable candidate being found. This directly hurts the education of US students as well; so many of my mentors and peers have been international and have shared their passion for and knowledge of science with me.
This proposed fee would harm US workers by wasting taxpayer money and by resulting in the loss of international talent which is necessary to educate US students and complete projects marked as a priority by being funded by the US government.
I recommend the agency remove the fee altogether; but, if a fee must be in place to offset costs, the agency should keep it at the current roughly $500 filing fee to not waste taxpayer money.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Kelly P.
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and a $30,000 fee for subsequent recommendations. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal because of the significant harm it would cause to international students, U.S. higher education institutions, and the American economy.
I have served as a Principal Designated School Official (PDSO) at various higher education institutions for more than a decade, working directly with international students and overseeing compliance with federal immigration regulations. Throughout my career, I have witnessed firsthand the importance of OPT as an integral part of international students' educational and professional development. OPT provides students with opportunities to apply their academic knowledge while contributing their skills and talents to U.S. businesses, research institutions, and communities.
The proposed fees would effectively make OPT inaccessible to most, if not all, students and institutions. Many institutions simply cannot absorb such extraordinary costs and would be forced to stop recommending otherwise eligible students for OPT. This would particularly harm students who have already invested substantial resources in their U.S. education with the expectation of gaining practical experience after graduation.
Furthermore, DSOs are neither equipped nor authorized to make subjective determinations about which eligible students are more academically deserving of OPT opportunities than others. Their responsibility is to verify regulatory eligibility and maintain compliance, not to determine which students merit an institution's extraordinary financial investment. Institutions and international student offices also lack the administrative and financial mechanisms necessary to collect, process, and remit payments of this magnitude for individual OPT recommendations. The proposal would place DSOs and institutions in an untenable position, effectively transforming a regulatory eligibility determination into a financial decision.
I am also deeply concerned about DHS's justification for these fees as a means of combating alleged fraud and protecting program integrity. Under the proposal, the revenue collected would be deposited into the general U.S. Treasury rather than dedicated to OPT oversight, fraud investigations, or enforcement. Consequently, there is no assurance that these substantial payments would fund any measures to address the very concerns DHS cites to justify them. Charging compliant institutions exorbitant fees without directing those resources toward fraud prevention does not meaningfully address the underlying issues. Existing SEVIS reporting requirements, institutional oversight, and STEM OPT compliance mechanisms already provide opportunities for more targeted enforcement.
The broader consequences would be substantial. OPT is an important factor in international students' decisions to pursue education in the United States. Restricting access would discourage enrollment, undermine institutional finances, and negatively affect academic programs, research, and employment opportunities for American faculty and staff. International students also contribute billions of dollars to the U.S. economy through tuition, living expenses, and workforce participation. Making OPT financially inaccessible would weaken U.S. competitiveness and encourage talented students to pursue opportunities in other countries.
After more than a decade working in international education, I am deeply concerned that this proposal would undermine a longstanding educational benefit while imposing unreasonable financial and administrative burdens on institutions. I strongly urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and instead pursue targeted, evidence-based measures that address documented compliance concerns without jeopardizing international students' futures, institutional sustainability, and the economic contributions of international education.
Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal due to its harm.

I am an F-1 graduate currently working in the United States on post-completion Optional Practical Training (OPT). If this pathway becomes unaffordable or unavailable, far fewer international students will come, and fewer still will stay. International students contribute tens of billions of dollars a year to the U.S. economy and pay tuition that helps sustain university budgets, research programs, and services that American students also rely on. A sharp drop in international enrollment would leave many institutions unable to maintain their current operations.

The same problem applies to the $30,000 fee for each subsequent recommendation: it directly discourages STEM OPT extensions, penalizing graduates who have followed every rule and are working in the fields where the United States says it wants to retain talent.

First, I would like to clarify an important misconception regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT), as the process does not work as described in the proposed rule.

Designated School Officials (DSOs) do not select or determine which students are allowed to participate in OPT. Their role is to verify that international students have successfully completed, or are on track to complete, their academic program and meet the eligibility requirements to apply for OPT. USCIS is the agency responsible for reviewing, processing, and approving OPT applications.

Once USCIS approves an application and the student receives their Employment Authorization Document (EAD), the student can begin seeking employment directly related to their field of study. DSOs subsequently help ensure that the reported employment meets the regulatory requirements and is related to the student's academic degree.

The process is straightforward, and it is important to understand that receiving OPT authorization does not guarantee employment. Many international students are unable to secure jobs within their authorized period. As a result, some choose to pursue another academic degree, while others return to their home countries.

OPT is not a program designed to take jobs away from U.S. citizens. Rather, it provides international graduates with an opportunity to gain practical experience directly related to the education they received in the United States. Many of these graduates eventually return to their home countries, taking with them the knowledge, skills, and professional experience acquired through American higher education.

Furthermore, international students make significant contributions to the U.S. economy. They generate substantial economic activity through tuition payments, housing, transportation, groceries, retail purchases, and other everyday living expenses. According to Open Doors (Open Doors is sponsored by the U.S. Department of State with funding provided by the U.S. Government and supported in its implementation by IIE.), international students contributed nearly $55 billion to the U.S. economy in 2024 (https://opendoorsdata.org/services/research-special-reports-and-analyses/economic-impact-of-international-students/).

Approving this proposed rule could have consequences far beyond the international student population. It could negatively affect U.S. colleges and universities, reduce institutional revenue, discourage talented international students from choosing the United States as their destination for higher education, and ultimately weaken an important contributor to the American economy.

We must recognize that international education is not simply an immigration issue; it is also an educational and economic issue. International students contribute to our communities, support American jobs through their spending, strengthen our institutions of higher education, and help maintain the United States' global competitiveness.

Before implementing a policy that could significantly restrict OPT, it is essential to understand how the program actually operates and recognize the substantial educational and economic benefits it provides to the United States.

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule introducing a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 extension fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations. While maintaining program integrity and curbing fraud are critical objectives, this proposed fee structure is legally arbitrary, financially untenable for institutions and students, ineffective at preventing bad actors, and directly counterproductive to U.S. national security and economic priorities.

1. Lack of Statutory Justification and Cost-Accounting Basis
Under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and federal fee-setting guidelines (such as OMB Circular A-25), agency fees must be reasonably calculated to recover the administrative costs of providing a specific service.

Arbitrary Valuation: The proposed rule provides no transparent cost-accounting, empirical data, or mathematical framework explaining how DHS arrived at a $70,000 baseline or a $30,000 extension fee.

Regulatory Ambiguity: The proposed rule is dangerously vague regarding the operational application of the $30,000 extension fee—specifically whether it applies per attempt, per degree level, or sequentially across pre-completion, post-completion, and 24-month STEM OPT phases.

2. Untenable Cost Burden on Educational Institutions and Students.
Imposing a cumulative $100,000 burden per student places an insurmountable financial barrier on both higher education institutions and participants:

Higher Education Infrastructure: Higher education institutions cannot absorb multi-million-dollar annual fee liabilities to issue standard academic recommendations. Beyond the fees themselves, institutions will face substantial compliance costs to build payment collection mechanisms, hire operational staff, and manage software upgrades.

Students and Employers: Students—whether on financial aid or self-funded—cannot afford a $70,000 to $100,000 access fee for practical training. Employers participating in standard entry-level post-graduate training programs cannot justify paying six-figure surcharges for short-term, entry-level training roles.

3. Ineffective and Counterproductive as an Anti-Fraud Measure
The core rationale for this rule—using financial cost to deter fraud—is fundamentally flawed:

Inability to Pay does not equal Non-Compliance: Ability to pay high fees bears no correlation to legal compliance or integrity. Wealthy bad actors can easily pay a fee, whereas law-abiding, highly qualified candidates will be priced out.

Penalizing Compliant Students: The vast majority of F-1 students utilize OPT strictly within regulatory bounds to gain practical experience. This rule disproportionately punishes legitimate participants and restricts OPT availability almost exclusively to individuals securing immediate, high-paying corporate roles on an H-1B trajectory.

Socioeconomic Inequity: The fee creates a severe "have vs. have-not" system, restricting practical training to ultra-wealthy international students regardless of merit or academic achievements.

4. Severe Economic, Academic, and National Security Repercussions
Practical training is a key bridge between classroom learning and real-world innovation. Crushing this program damages broader U.S. interests:

Chilling Effect on U.S. Higher Education: Unprecedented fees will drive top international talent away from American universities toward competing nations (such as Canada, the UK, and Australia) with straightforward post-study work pathways.

Undermining U.S. Talent Retention Goals: OPT represents the nation's premier talent retention pipeline for top scientists, researchers, and engineers, particularly in critical STEM fields. Most international graduates return home, but those who stay often launch careers, build startups, and drive domestic innovation.

Conflict with Administration Priorities: A key goal of the White House is "attracting and retaining top-tier global talent" in industries vital to national security and critical technologies. As President Trump has publicly noted, international talent often struggles with visa uncertainty when deciding whether to launch their careers in the U.S. Placing a $100,000 price tag on OPT directly undermines the policy goal of keeping the world's best minds in America.

For these reasons, DHS should immediately withdraw the proposed $70,000 / $30,000 fee structure for OPT recommendations. The agency should instead focus on targeted, evidence-based compliance monitoring that preserves the vital role of practical training in American higher education and global competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly support the proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for any subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT extensions. These fees are a necessary step to protect American workers, reduce fraud, and restore integrity to a program that has grown into a large-scale, uncapped guest-worker pathway.

OPT has expanded dramatically, with roughly 294,000 participants in the 2024/25 academic year according to Open Doors data, and hundreds of thousands of authorizations in SEVIS. Unlike H-1B, OPT has no annual numerical limit, no comparable prevailing-wage requirement, and no labor-market test requiring employers to try hiring Americans first. It is concentrated in STEM fields, particularly computer science and related disciplines, where recent American graduates have faced elevated unemployment even as OPT participation in those same fields has grown substantially.

Employers receive a structural cost advantage when hiring OPT participants. Because these workers are generally non-resident aliens, both the employee and employer are typically exempt from FICA taxes (Social Security and Medicare). This creates an estimated 7–15% payroll cost savings relative to hiring a comparable U.S. citizen or permanent resident. In competitive entry-level STEM roles, this tax subsidy systematically tilts hiring decisions against American graduates. The program’s concentration among large technology employers further concentrates competitive pressure on younger American workers seeking their first professional positions.

DHS and ICE have documented extensive fraud and abuse, including more than 10,000 potential fraud cases involving “pay-to-stay” schemes, shell employers, remote or offshore management of purported U.S. training, and worksites that do not provide genuine training. Schools currently face limited financial consequences for recommending large numbers of students, which weakens incentives for rigorous oversight by designated school officials. Placing a substantial fee on the recommending institution before the SEVIS recommendation and USCIS employment-authorization process creates accountability. It encourages schools to be more selective, improves program integrity, and reduces the volume of cases that exploit the system as a de facto work visa.

A $70,000 / $30,000 structure is meaningful relative to current practice, under which schools pay no OPT recommendation fee. However, given the scale of the program, the documented fraud, the multi-year duration of many OPT periods (especially STEM extensions), and the ongoing tax advantage conferred on employers, the fees may still be insufficient to fully internalize the costs imposed on American workers and the immigration system. Higher fees, or a structure that more closely tracks the economic value of the work authorization and the associated enforcement burden, would further deter marginal or fraudulent participation while preserving genuine, high-value training opportunities. Fees deposited to the Treasury also help offset the administrative and investigative costs of a program that has grown far beyond its original training purpose.

The proposal correctly places the fee on SEVP-certified schools rather than directly on students or tying it to a specific employer. This aligns incentives at the point of recommendation—the stage where institutional knowledge and control are highest—and avoids creating new barriers that could be easily gamed at the individual level.

I urge DHS to finalize the rule substantially as proposed and to consider whether modestly higher fees would better achieve the stated goals of combating fraud, strengthening system integrity, and protecting U.S. workers from unfair competition created by an uncapped program with a built-in tax subsidy. American graduates should compete on merit, not against a regulatory structure that systematically advantages foreign students through lower costs and fewer labor protections. This rule is a constructive step in that direction.

DHS should withdraw the proposed OPT fee because its costs outweigh its benefits. The rule would charge schools ab $70,000 for a student's first period of OPT and $30,000 for each later one. Many schools, students, and employers cannot absorb that cost. Schools that refuse to pay would end practical training for their students, and schools that pay would likely recover the cost through higher tuition for all students or charges to employers. Without it, many would go to countries that let graduates work after their studies. American schools would then lose tuition that helps support domestic students and research. Employers would lose graduates trained here, including in fields where qualified workers are hard to find, and some would move that work abroad. Local economies would lose the spending, tax revenue, and new businesses these graduates bring. The fee also applies to OPT taken during school. If the recent limits on curricular practical training stand, OPT would be the only way for many students to gain work experience before graduation, yet the fee would give schools a strong reason to refuse it. The benefits do not make up for these costs.

The rule's first stated goal is to combat fraud, such as shell companies that sell false job letters to students. But the fee is charged to schools, not to shell companies. It falls mostly on students who follow the rules. Targeted tools, such as employer verification, training plans, and site visits, would reach fraud directly without charging honest students, and DHS already uses them for STEM OPT.

The rule also does little to protect American workers. When a company cannot hire a graduate it needs, the job often moves abroad or goes unfilled. The fee would not fund better oversight either, because the money would go to the general Treasury rather than to the program. A rule should be adopted only when its benefits justify its costs and no cheaper option would meet the same goal. This proposal does not meet that standard. DHS should withdraw it or, at minimum, exempt OPT taken during school and rely on targeted enforcement.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I write in opposition to the proposed rule requiring SEVP-certified schools to pay $70,000 before recommending a student’s initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions. I urge DHS to withdraw it. I am a current student with experience receiving OPT multiple times in the past.

I recognize that DHS has legitimate interests in preventing fraud, protecting U.S. workers, and ensuring appropriate oversight of OPT. My objection is that this rule does not serve those interests. It is the wrong tool, set at the wrong price, with too little explanation.

1. The fees bear no relationship to any identified cost. Government fees ordinarily recover the cost of a service. A DSO’s OPT recommendation is an entry in SEVIS, and USCIS separately charges its own adjudication fee. A $70,000 charge for that entry cannot plausibly be cost recovery. If schools should contribute to the program’s integrity costs, that argues for a fee tied to actual administrative expense. The proposal also appears to direct revenue to the general treasury, and DHS should explain what statutory authority supports fees of this magnitude.

2. The rule would end OPT in practice, not merely regulate it. Few institutions can absorb a five-figure charge per student, and few students can pay it. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the cost to students, all students, or employers. A benefit available only to students who can pay $70,000 is a benefit in name only. If DHS or Congress intends to eliminate or sharply curtail OPT, that decision should be made openly and on its merits, not through a fee structure that achieves the same result.

3. Fraud concerns call for targeted enforcement. Fraud should be punished, but this rule charges every school and every student, including the overwhelming majority who comply. A $70,000 fee does not distinguish a legitimate university from a sham one; it mostly deters the compliant. DHS already has tools aimed at bad actors: SEVP can withdraw school certification, ICE can investigate and enforce, and employers have reporting obligations. Stronger use of those tools would address fraud directly without penalizing lawful participants.

4. Labor-market concerns should be answered with evidence. OPT is limited in duration and tied to the student’s field of study. If DHS believes OPT displaces U.S. workers or depresses wages, it should publish that analysis and propose measures matched to the findings. A prohibitive fee is not such a measure. Many employers report using OPT and STEM OPT to fill hard-to-staff technical roles, and international graduates frequently start companies that create U.S. jobs.

5. The fee adds no worker protections. STEM OPT already requires a formal training plan and employer reporting. If DHS sees gaps in oversight, it can tighten those requirements directly. Charging schools does not change how employers treat workers or improve training quality.

6. Schools cannot simply absorb the cost, and many are not wealthy. DHS may view institutions as beneficiaries of international enrollment, but the fee would fall on public universities, regional colleges, and smaller institutions that have the least capacity to bear it. International tuition often helps sustain programs and research that benefit domestic students as well. For a benefit that primarily serves the student and the employer, schools have no practical way to recover this cost except by raising costs on students.

7. The rule is unclear on a critical point. The text is ambiguous about whether there is a cap on how many times a school must pay for the same student. Institutions cannot budget, set tuition, or advise students without knowing their potential liability. A rule imposing costs of this scale must be precise.

8. The broader harm falls on the United States. International students pay tuition, support research, and fill roles in fields facing shortages. OPT is a major reason they choose the United States over Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia. Making it unaffordable will redirect talent and economic activity abroad, and employers, especially small and mid-sized businesses without other visa options, will lose access to trained graduates.

9. The comment period is too short. A rule of this scale, affecting thousands of institutions and many thousands of students and employers, warrants more than 30 days. DHS should extend the period and publish the data and economic analysis on which it relies.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS proceeds, it should substantially reduce the fees to reflect actual administrative costs, clarify any cap on repeat payments, pursue its fraud and oversight goals through targeted measures, and provide an extended comment period.

The proposed OPT fee structure should be evaluated not only for its financial effects on educational institutions, but also for its administrative efficiency and enforcement value.

Three questions require particular attention.

1. What measurable compliance improvement is expected?

A substantial fee may reduce participation in OPT, but reduced participation is not equivalent to reduced fraud. The Department should distinguish between legitimate applications that become financially impractical and fraudulent arrangements prevented through enforcement.

2. Are the fees proportionate to the regulatory objective?

The Department should provide a transparent explanation of the relationship between the proposed payment amounts, administrative requirements, and anticipated compliance benefits.

Without that analysis, it is difficult to determine whether the fee structure is a cost-effective regulatory instrument.

3. Have less burdensome alternatives been adequately compared?

Employer verification, risk-based audits, improved reporting systems, and investigations focused on documented violations may address specific compliance problems.

These alternatives should be assessed against the proposed fees using consistent criteria, including enforcement effectiveness, administrative cost, institutional burden, and effects on lawful participation.

The proposed provisions under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) raise important questions about whether financial barriers are being used in place of direct compliance oversight.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee provisions and provide a more comprehensive comparison of regulatory alternatives.

Effective public administration requires demonstrating that a proposed intervention addresses the identified problem at a reasonable cost.

A regulation should be judged by its measurable outcomes, not simply by the magnitude of the financial obligation it imposes.

When people talk about OPT, the conversation usually focuses on engineers, scientists, and technology companies.

But what about the creative industries?

American businesses also employ people in animation, digital media, visual effects, interactive design, architecture, and other creative fields.

These careers depend heavily on practical experience. A student can learn design principles or animation software in college, but professional development involves collaborating with teams, meeting production deadlines, responding to client feedback, and understanding how creative projects are delivered.

OPT offers eligible international graduates an opportunity to develop those skills after completing their American education.

The proposed fees could make that transition considerably more difficult.

Smaller design studios, independent production companies, and creative agencies often operate with limited budgets. If universities become less willing to support OPT recommendations, these employers may face a narrower pool of qualified graduates.

I understand that immigration enforcement is necessary. However, I question whether imposing substantial fees on educational institutions is an effective way to identify fraudulent training arrangements.

The ability to pay does not demonstrate that a student is properly trained or that an employer is operating legitimately.

I also believe the economic analysis should recognize that American competitiveness extends beyond scientific research and traditional manufacturing.

Creative industries produce intellectual property, develop commercial products, and contribute to America's cultural influence internationally.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee provisions under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) and consider more targeted compliance measures.

The economic consequences of this proposal should be examined across the full range of industries that rely on professionally trained graduates, including fields that are often overlooked in immigration policy discussions.

Veterans returning to civilian life may need specialized services involving physical rehabilitation, mental health support, prosthetic technology, vocational training, and assistance with disabilities. This does not mean that veterans' services depend entirely on international graduates. They do not. However, workforce policies can have indirect consequences for organizations that serve veterans and their families.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee provisions under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2), and consider targeted verification and compliance enforcement instead.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Rene Villarreal
comments.commentText:
This is a completely inappropriate, unnecessary, and counterintuitive announcement that further damages the reputation of the United States amongst global communities. Not only do F-1 students engaged with OPT bolster the United States' economy, but the relationships that they build progress diplomatic relationships between nations. Increasing the financial burden of this legal benefit of the F-1 visa is extremely damaging to the United States economy and the ability for educational institutions to function, as this proposed charge is incommensurate to what institutions or students can afford and ignores preexisting legal framework already agreed upon and implemented.

The legality of this rule will be challenged in court, just as the disproportionate charges surrounding H1B visa-holders was. This costs money while, at the same time as a result of this thoughtless proposal, the US economy will suffer from a loss of potential employment. Citizens will not replace these positions; as we have seen, these positions will cease to exist, plummeting the US economy further.

The system to properly and legally vet OPT applicants is already in place. Adding a financial requirement, and a disproportionate one at that, on top of the legally agreed filing fee, which already exists for OPT, will cause more damage to the United States than what is currently in place, as many students already struggle to afford the filing fee already in place. This already acts as a hurdle for students to apply for OPT, and raising the hurdle 100x the existing fee is not legally justifiable.

If passed, this proposal would set the dangerous precedence that education and employment are only available to those who are already wealthy, AND this proposal directly contradicts previously, legally agreed upon regulations for this legal benefit of the F-1 visa. There is no logical, humane, or otherwise sound reason for this proposal.

I strongly recommend that the DHS reconsiders this proposal and begins to restaff USCIS, as this agency, and the lag time for adjudication, actually creates more uncertainty and more possibility for abuse of the F-1 visa by not processing legal benefits of the visa, i.e. OPT and STEM OPT, within the allotted time frame for adjudication. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. As an international student who has lived and studied in the United States for almost ten years, I believe this proposal would create substantial barriers to professional training, discourage international talent from contributing to the American workforce, and ultimately harm U.S. economic competitiveness.

I came to the United States nearly a decade ago to pursue higher education. Since then, I have completed undergraduate and graduate studies in chemical engineering and am currently pursuing a Ph.D. in environmental engineering at a U.S. university. Throughout these years, I have invested significant time and effort in developing technical expertise, conducting scientific research, and preparing to contribute to society through engineering. The opportunity to apply this training in American industries has been an important part of my educational and professional aspirations.

In engineering, classroom education and academic research alone cannot fully prepare students for professional practice. Curricular Practical Training (CPT) and OPT provide invaluable opportunities to apply theoretical knowledge to real-world industrial challenges, understand industrial operations, develop professional skills, and collaborate with engineers from diverse backgrounds. My own industrial experiences have helped me understand how engineering principles are translated into practical technologies and solutions, something that cannot be fully replicated in a classroom or academic laboratory.

For students in chemical and environmental engineering, such experiences are especially important. Our expertise directly supports industries addressing challenges in environmental protection, sustainable manufacturing, energy efficiency, and industrial innovation. Through practical training, international students can contribute specialized knowledge and fresh perspectives while developing the experience necessary to become effective engineers and researchers.

Although the proposed fees formally apply to educational institutions rather than individual students, their consequences would directly affect students like me. A $70,000 initial fee, potentially followed by another $30,000 for a STEM OPT extension, creates an extraordinary financial barrier. Universities may be unable or unwilling to absorb these costs, and passing them on to students or employers would make practical training inaccessible for many qualified students. OPT is often the primary pathway for international graduates to gain professional experience and begin their careers in the United States. Without an affordable and accessible OPT program, students may lose employment opportunities despite having successfully completed years of education and training at American universities.

Personally, this proposal introduces significant uncertainty into my career planning. After spending nearly a decade building my education, research expertise, and professional connections in the United States, I hope to apply my skills to solving real engineering challenges in the American workforce. Under the proposed rule, my ability to pursue this goal could depend not on my qualifications, skills, or potential contributions, but on whether my university can justify paying an exceptionally high fee for my participation in OPT. This would be deeply discouraging for students who have devoted years to preparing for careers in the United States.

The consequences also extend far beyond individual students. American universities attract talented students from around the world, train them in advanced scientific and engineering disciplines, and prepare them to contribute to American industries. These students bring technical expertise, support research and innovation, contribute to local economies, and help American companies remain competitive internationally. OPT provides an essential bridge between this educational investment and its economic returns. Making that bridge prohibitively expensive risks encouraging talented graduates to pursue their careers in other countries instead.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements and preserve accessible practical training opportunities for international students. The United States has invested in educating generations of international scientists and engineers. Allowing these individuals to apply their training and contribute to American industries benefits not only the students themselves, but also the U.S. economy, technological leadership, and society as a whole.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed high OPT fees, arguing they create barriers and harm U.S. competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT) and to urge the Department to withdraw them.

International students are a proven economic engine for the United States. In the 2024-2025 academic year, international students at U.S. colleges and universities contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs. For every three international students, one U.S. job is created or supported. That spending reaches local landlords, restaurants, retailers, and campus payrolls. It is also already declining. NAFSA estimates the U.S. economy lost $1.1 billion and nearly 23,000 jobs in Fall 2025 alone due to shrinking international student numbers. Adding new costs to OPT would deepen that lose.

OPT is not a side benefit of studying in the United States. For many students, it is the reason they choose a U.S. university over one in Canada, the United Kingdom, or Australia. At the University at Buffalo, our office oversaw 4,631 students on OPT and STEM OPT in Fall 2025, more than the 3,820 F-1 and J-1 students enrolled on campus. These graduates are working for American employers right now.

The stakes are highest in artificial intelligence and technology. According to the National Foundation for American Policy, 70% of full-time graduate students at U.S. universities in AI-related fields are international students. The same research found that 42% of major AI companies in the United States have a founder who came to the U.S. as an international student. OPT is the bridge between those classrooms and those companies. Making that bridge more expensive hands an advantage to countries competing with the United States for AI leadership, including China, which would welcome the talent we discourage.

International students also shape what an American education is. Domestic students learn alongside peers from more than a hundred countries and graduate with the cross-cultural skills U.S. employers increasingly expect. International graduates who build early careers here through OPT often become long-term partners to American businesses and research institutions, whether they stay in the United States or return home.

These students and their families have already invested tens of thousands of dollars in U.S. tuition and living costs. A new fee at the point of graduation penalizes them for completing the education they came here to pursue, and it signals to future students that the United States is becoming more expensive and less welcoming than its competitors.

The proposed fees would harm students, universities, employers, and American workers who benefit from this talent. I urge DHS to withdraw them and preserve a fair and accessible OPT program.
