comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. Charging schools $70,000 for a student’s first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each one after, including STEM OPT, would function as a near-ban on practical training for most international students. That would weaken the U.S. economy, cost American jobs, and push skilled people we have already trained to build their careers in competing countries.

International students strengthen the U.S. economy. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in the 2024-25 academic year, roughly one U.S. job for every three international students. In Illinois alone, that meant $2.4 billion and 22,479 jobs. These are jobs held by Americans in housing, retail, dining, transportation, and on campuses.

That contribution is already shrinking. NAFSA estimates that a 17 percent drop in new international enrollment in fall 2025 cost the U.S. economy over $1.1 billion and nearly 23,000 jobs. This rule would deepen that decline. Students choose where to study partly on whether they can gain work experience afterward: in a May 2026 IDP Education survey of nearly 6,000 international students, 66 percent said they would go elsewhere or consider going elsewhere without post-study work opportunities. Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Germany will gladly take them.

DHS’s own analysis points the same way. In 2024, 194,554 students began OPT and 95,384 began STEM OPT. DHS’s low-end estimate projects a 56 percent decline in OPT participation under this rule, and it estimates tens of billions of dollars in economic costs over ten years while quantifying no offsetting benefits.

The rule’s premise, that OPT takes jobs from Americans, is not supported by evidence. A 2023 Niskanen Center study found that practical training for foreign STEM students is linked to more innovation and higher average earnings without displacing U.S. workers or lowering their wages. A 2019 National Foundation for American Policy analysis found no evidence that OPT reduces job opportunities for U.S. workers. Talented graduates create jobs: they fill shortages, start companies, and make the teams around them more productive. If DHS is concerned about fraud by specific employers, it already has targeted tools, including SEVIS reporting and site visits. A six-figure fee charged to every school for every student is not a fraud measure. It punishes the many for the misconduct of a few.

International students also bring something harder to put a dollar figure on. They sit in classrooms with American students, work alongside American colleagues, and build lasting personal and professional ties between the United States and the rest of the world. That global understanding is a national asset, and it depends on students being able to stay, work, and contribute after graduation.

This issue is personal for me. My mother needed brain surgery. The neurosurgeon who saved her life came to the United States as an F-1 student, gained experience through OPT, and later stayed on an H-1B visa. Without OPT, that pathway would not have existed, and my mother would not be alive today. Behind the statistics are doctors, engineers, researchers, and entrepreneurs whose work directly protects and improves the lives of American citizens. Making it prohibitively expensive for them to begin their careers here does not protect Americans. It puts us at risk.

This proposal is shortsighted. It will cost American jobs, weaken American universities, and hand our competitors the talent we spent years educating. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the rule in its entirety and to keep OPT and STEM OPT accessible without these fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Oliver Rosand
comments.commentText:
I am a law student, and I write to oppose DHS’s proposal to charge schools $70,000 for a student’s first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one, including STEM OPT extensions.

International students are part of American universities’ classrooms, labs, and clinics, and part of the legal profession. Under this rule, the decision about whether a student who meets every legal requirement can train in their field would no longer turn on merit or eligibility. It would turn on whether the student’s school decides to spend $70,000 on that student. DHS says outright that it expects schools to recommend only “the most promising” students. In practice, wealthy institutions and wealthy students would continue to have access, and everyone else would lose it.

OPT is one of the main reasons international students choose U.S. universities over competitors in Canada, the U.K., and Europe. A fee that can reach $100,000 per student would make U.S. programs much less attractive and would hit graduate and STEM programs hardest. Fewer international students means fewer research collaborators, fewer people to staff labs and teach, and less tuition supporting the programs that U.S. students attend as well. U.S. employers would lose access to graduates they have already spent time recruiting and training.

OPT and STEM OPT participants work in fields where the country needs talent: medicine and public health, engineering, computing, and scientific research. Pushing that talent to other countries weakens innovation and economic growth in the United States and gives competing countries an advantage in recruiting the world’s best students.

The rule is legally flawed. DHS relies on INA § 214(a). That provision lets DHS set conditions for nonimmigrant status. It does not let DHS raise revenue. The proposed amounts have no connection to what it costs DHS to process an OPT recommendation, and the money would go to the Treasury’s general fund. DHS’s own estimate is $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year. A charge like that is a tax, and only Congress can impose taxes. National Cable Television Ass’n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974). The NPRM also never explains how DHS arrived at $70,000 or $30,000. And it never explains how a fee paid before any employer is identified would address fraud, which typically involves sham employers. DHS already has targeted tools for that, including SEVIS reporting, employer attestations, and site visits. Finally, a 30-day comment period is too short for a rule with economic effects this large.

My request. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. If it does not, it should reopen the comment period for at least 60 more days.

Respectfully submitted.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees harm students, institutions, and the U.S. economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The foundational strength of our nation lies in its history as a melting pot—a place where the best and brightest minds from across the globe come together to innovate, build, and drive our shared prosperity. Restricting overseas talent through steep, punitive financial barriers undermines this exact tradition and directly hurts our domestic economy.
The assertion that foreign talent harms local labor market outcomes is contradicted by economic data. High-skilled immigrants do not replace domestic workers; they expand the broader economic pie:
* Job Creation & Entrepreneurship: Immigrants start companies at higher rates than native-born citizens. Nationwide, over 3 million foreign-born entrepreneurs employ nearly 8 million local workers. Furthermore, research consistently shows that adding skilled workers—particularly in STEM fields—creates complementary job growth for native workers in surrounding sectors.
* Net Fiscal Contributions: High-skilled immigrants represent an extraordinary net benefit to public finances. According to the Manhattan Institute, a college-educated foreign worker arriving at a young age generates hundreds of thousands of dollars in net tax contributions over their lifetime, paying far more in income, payroll, and corporate taxes than they consume in public benefits.
* Innovation & Global Competitiveness: Immigrants are listed as inventors on a disproportionate share of U.S. patents—over 75% at top research universities. Imposing arbitrary $100k fees forces high-growth companies to offshore research, engineering, and product development hubs to countries with more open talent pipelines.
When we create friction for international talent, we do not protect domestic jobs; we stifle innovation and cut off tax revenues that fund public services. To turn away skilled talent is to reject the core economic principles that made our nation a global leader. Rather than closing our doors and going backward, we should continue attracting top global talent to build a flourishing, competitive future.

I submit this comment as an individual citizen. I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and the $30,000 fee for subsequent recommendations.

These fees would make OPT inaccessible to many students. Standard OPT is not tied to having an employer at the time of application; students may apply without a job offer and may apply as early as 90 days before completing their degree. It is therefore unrealistic to expect students—or schools acting on their behalf—to pay tens of thousands of dollars when no employer may yet be available to share the cost.

The proposed initial fee could exceed the total cost of an entire academic year in the United States. Many graduate students rely on assistantships, stipends, or tuition support to finance their education and do not have access to $70,000 in personal or family funds. Although the fees would formally be charged to schools, institutions may pass the cost to students or decline to recommend them for OPT.

As a result, students may avoid OPT, and prospective international students may choose to study in other countries instead. Research cited in the public record estimates that the proposal could reduce OPT participation by approximately 80 percent in some scenarios, reduce international enrollment, and ultimately lower annual U.S. GDP by approximately $362 billion after ten years.

OPT connects U.S. education with the American workforce, supporting employers, research, innovation, and economic growth. Making the program financially inaccessible would undermine these benefits and weaken the United States’ ability to attract and retain international talent.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and pursue targeted measures to address fraud or noncompliance rather than imposing extraordinary costs on lawful students and institutions.

I am writing to oppose the proposed rule that would charge universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to focus on a contradiction at the center of this proposal: the administration has declared American leadership in artificial intelligence a national priority, and this rule taxes the very pipeline that produces it.

The United States does not lead in AI because it has a monopoly on talent. It leads because the world's most promising researchers come here to study, and OPT is the mechanism that keeps them here after graduation. A large share of the doctoral graduates in computer science and AI at American universities are international students, and a large share of the researchers staffing American AI labs — university labs, national laboratories, and private research groups — first worked in this country on OPT. The STEM extension, which this rule would surcharge by $30,000, is what gives a doctoral graduate the time to finish a research project, publish, and transition into the roles the country's AI strategy depends on.

Consider what happens when that bridge is priced out of reach. The graduate does not stop being an AI researcher. The graduate becomes an AI researcher in another country — in a lab in Toronto, London, or Shenzhen, working on the same problems, publishing the same papers, and building the competing systems that American policy is meant to outpace. The United States spent years and hundreds of thousands of dollars in educational investment training that person, and this rule would hand the return on that investment to its rivals. That is not a trade-off between immigration enforcement and innovation. It is a direct transfer of capability from the United States to its competitors.

The damage reaches beyond AI. The semiconductor workforce the CHIPS Act is trying to build, the biotech researchers, the engineers in advanced manufacturing — all draw on the same OPT pipeline. DHS estimates the fee would extract $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year from universities, and its own analysis concedes some schools would simply stop recommending OPT. When the recommendation stops, the graduate leaves, and the lab, the startup, or the national laboratory that would have employed them loses a worker it cannot easily replace.

A rule that claims to protect American workers while exporting the researchers who build American technology is working against its own stated purpose. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, which proposes a $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, and urge DHS to withdraw the rule.

DHS proposes a $70,000 “fee” for the initial filing for OPT per student, and an additional $30,000 for every subsequent OPT application filed per student. DHS further proposes that “the proposed OPT fees collected under this rule would be deposited in the Treasury of the United States as a miscellaneous receipt pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 3302” (p.64577). A fee is generally understood as payments charged to cover the costs of providing a good or service, charged specifically for the beneficiaries of those services (415 U.S. 352 (1974)), an example of this being the OPT filing fee and premium processing service fee that USCIS charges applicants. In contrast, a tax is a compulsory payment applied equally across populations and places for the purpose of funding the provision of public goods (112 U.S. 580 (1884)). The revenue earned from the tax being deposited in the General Treasury rather than DHS or ICE, and the parties bearing the expense of the “fee” being institutions rather than the OPT applicant directly imply that the amount will be treated as tax revenue rather than the cost of providing a specific service. We argue that this is a misrepresentation of the intended purpose of the fee, and does not serve to combat fraud or protect American workers as DHS claims it does.

DHS also claims that “The financial costs would deter schools from recommending students with questionable qualifications for OPT, leading to higher program integrity. DHS anticipates that schools will consider adopting internal policies and procedures that prioritize quality and compliance over quantity of participants, stabilizing the number of OPT participants.” (p.64575). The proposed rule lays out no guidance on what DHS considers “questionable qualifications”, nor what parameters institutions are supposed to adopt. We are concerned that such an ambiguous instruction is encouraging schools to partake in actions violating Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color, and national origin in programs and activities receiving federal financial assistance. OPT is a training program available to every F-1 student that complies with the eligibility guidelines, and it is unfair and unjust to ask institutions to undertake discriminatory practices merely to issue recommendations for an authorization we do not grant.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I submit this comment anonymously as a member of the public concerned about the effects of this proposal on international students, universities, and employers.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule, including proposed 8 C.F.R. §§ 214.13(i)(1)–(3) and 214.2(f)(11)(ii)–(iii). A $70,000 fee for a student’s first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation would make practical training unavailable to many students and lead schools to ration access based on funding rather than a student’s qualifications, educational goals, or the legitimacy of a job.

The fee is not tied to a particular employer or a specific investigation. It applies whether a student seeks pre-completion or post-completion OPT, and applies again to later OPT recommendations, including STEM OPT. A school must pay before it can recommend a student. That structure places the burden on universities before a student can work, even when the school has no control over the student’s eventual employer and the student has complied with all program requirements. DHS’s own analysis estimates annual fee transfers of $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion. (91 Fed. Reg. 64583–84.) These figures underscore that the proposal is not calibrated to the administrative cost of reviewing a recommendation.

The proposal would also distort students’ academic and career choices. DHS anticipates that schools may be less likely to pay the initial fee for students eligible for only one year of OPT than for students eligible for a STEM extension, and that students may shift from pre-completion to post-completion OPT to avoid paying twice. (91 Fed. Reg. 64583–84.) Students should be able to choose training and employment based on their education and career development, not on whether their school can absorb a six-figure cost or whether a particular degree makes the fee seem financially worthwhile. Those unable to secure OPT may lose employment opportunities, income, and the chance to build professional experience in the United States.

The proposal would also make U.S. universities less attractive to talented international students. Students deciding where to study must consider whether they can pursue lawful, degree-related work after graduation. A fee of this scale creates serious uncertainty for students and universities alike, and could discourage enrollment and reduce the diversity of perspectives in classrooms, research groups, and professional workplaces. The costs may be shifted to students, employers, or the broader student body, so the burden could fall even on people who never seek OPT.

DHS identifies fraud and limited oversight resources as the problems it seeks to address. Those concerns merit an effective response, but a blanket fee does not distinguish fraudulent activity from legitimate training. It risks excluding compliant students while failing to target the employers and intermediaries responsible for abuse. DHS should instead use targeted investigations, employer oversight, reporting requirements, and enforcement against proven violations. DHS itself considered expanded site visits and reporting requirements but rejected them without demonstrating that a fee of this magnitude would better identify or prevent fraud. (91 Fed. Reg. 64596.)

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees. At a minimum, DHS should not finalize them without establishing a reasoned connection between the fee amounts and the costs or oversight needs they are meant to address, assessing the effects on students and universities, and considering targeted alternatives that preserve access for compliant students.

Dear Department of Homeland Security Officer，

I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

International education is an essential component of the U.S. higher education system and plays a significant role in supporting the American economy. International students contribute far beyond tuition payments. They support universities financially, contribute to academic research and scientific innovation, fill important workforce needs, and bring diverse perspectives and expertise to American communities.

According to NAFSA: Association of International Educators, international students contributed approximately $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year. These figures demonstrate that international education is not simply an educational exchange; it is also an important economic contributor to the United States.

Although the proposed fees would technically be paid by educational institutions rather than directly by individual students, the financial burden would likely have significant consequences for both universities and international students. A fee of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation, followed by $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation, could make it financially unsustainable for many institutions to support international students seeking practical training opportunities. Universities may consequently limit OPT recommendations, reduce their willingness to enroll international students, or redirect resources away from other important educational and research activities.

More importantly, such a policy could substantially discourage prospective international students from choosing the United States as their study destination. International students make important decisions about where to pursue higher education based not only on academic quality but also on their opportunities to gain professional experience and apply their education after graduation. If the United States becomes significantly less accessible and less welcoming to international talent, students may increasingly choose other countries that offer more reasonable pathways from education to employment.

The potential consequences extend well beyond individual students. A decline in international student enrollment could reduce university revenues, affect university-supported employment, weaken research capacity, and limit the availability of highly educated talent for American employers. It could also negatively affect local economies, including housing, transportation, retail, and other businesses that benefit from international student spending. Over time, these effects could undermine the global competitiveness of American universities and the United States' ability to attract and retain talented individuals from around the world.

I recognize the importance of preventing fraud, maintaining the integrity of the immigration system, and protecting American workers. However, these objectives should be pursued through targeted compliance measures, stronger oversight, and reasonable administrative fees rather than imposing extraordinarily high fees that could discourage legitimate international students and create substantial financial barriers for educational institutions. A policy intended to protect the U.S. workforce should also consider the valuable contributions that international graduates make to that workforce and to the broader economy.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees or, at a minimum, substantially reconsider the proposed fee structure and conduct a more comprehensive assessment of its potential long-term economic, educational, and workforce consequences.

comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am writing to express my concerns regarding the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

First, while I recognize the importance of preventing immigration fraud, I question how imposing substantial fees on universities would effectively address the fraudulent employers and fictitious employment arrangements identified in the proposal. Legitimate students and fraudulent participants would face the same financial requirements, regardless of their compliance with immigration regulations. I ask DHS to provide evidence demonstrating that these fees would reduce fraud more effectively than targeted employer verification, stronger reporting requirements, and increased enforcement.

Second, I am concerned about the economic justification for the specific fee amounts. The proposal estimates substantial fee collections but acknowledges uncertainty surrounding the economic consequences of reduced OPT participation. How were the $70,000 and $30,000 amounts determined, and what evidence establishes that fees of this magnitude are necessary? I urge DHS to more fully evaluate the potential losses in research productivity, university enrollment, and contributions to the U.S. economy.

Third, this proposal would directly affect legitimate research opportunities. After graduation, many students may work in research positions at U.S. universities. The proposed initial OPT fee would sometimes exceed their annual salary, creating a substantial financial barrier to a legitimate research position. I ask DHS to consider how the rule would affect academic laboratories, nonprofit research institutions, and other organizations that rely on early-career researchers.

Finally, students like myself have invested years of education, financial resources, and career planning under existing OPT regulations. I ask DHS to more thoroughly evaluate these reliance interests and explain why the proposed 60-day transition period would be sufficient for currently enrolled students.

I respectfully request that DHS address these concerns, provide stronger evidence supporting the proposed fee amounts, and consider less burdensome alternatives before proceeding with a final rule.

Thank you for your consideration.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Acting Director David J. Venturella,

I submit this comment letter in response to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (Department) proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees (DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100), published October 8, 2026.

We oppose the proposed rule and urge that the proposed rule be withdrawn in its entirety, and that the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program remains intact.

DHS notes that “STEM OPT employers are subject to self-reporting requirements on the Form I-983, including certifying that the F-1 nonimmigrant student will not replace a U.S. worker...However, the employers for STEM OPT are not required to submit any business documents or supporting documents to DHS, such as tax records or proof of business.” (p.64574)

The need for greater transparency from employers and hiring practices is presented as a rationale for combating alleged OPT fraud. However, the fee imposed places a burden on institutions, despite no clear evidence that SEVP-certified institutions play any role in alleged OPT fraud. Furthermore, DHS provides no reasonable explanation for why it cannot update existing regulations and requirements for OPT employers as a measure against fraud. It also does not identify why the current information collected through SEVP, E-Verify, and the existing I-983 form is insufficient to investigate fraud, and why the additional information specified above is crucial to identifying fraud. We believe DHS has not made an attempt to explore less burdensome alternatives to the problem it poses in this proposal.

DHS presents the following statistic: “In fact, only about 20 percent of F-1 nonimmigrants participated in OPT in 2024 out of the 1.4 million F-1 nonimmigrants in the higher education system, which demonstrates that the vast majority of F-1 nonimmigrants choose to study in the United States for reasons other than to pursue work through OPT."” (p.64579). A September 2026 study examines the effects of this proposed tax on the price elasticity of demand for US degrees, university supply of OPT placements, and of employers’ demand for OPT workers. The results of this study showed that the nationwide count of international enrollment in the US responds with a price elasticity demand of -0.5 to -0.6, showing a fairly significant decline in enrollment in response to higher OPT taxes. It also demonstrated that when the $100,000 tax is offloaded onto students directly, the count for those starting OPT falls by a third of the no-tax baseline for OPT starters, and when the cost was borne by universities, OPT starts decline by four-fifths of the original baseline. This is preliminary evidence of the losses faced by universities and students with the imposition of this tax. [Source: https://docs.iza.org/dp18933.pdf]

One of the reasons presented by DHS as the basis of this rule is that OPT facilitates the undercutting worker wages and opportunities, go so far as to accuse the OPT program of “large scale replacement of American workers” (p. 64575). The Economic Innovation Group notes that international students transitioning to H-1B are more likely to add well-paying jobs to the US labor market, considering H-1Bs hired through outsourcing firms earn about $9,000 less than international students-turned-H-1B on average, despite being six years older than the latter group. [Source: https://agglomerations.eig.org/p/a-100000-tax-on-foreign-students]. A research study conducted by Seoyoung Kwon and Jongkwan Lee in March 2026 demonstrates that the increase in the supply of high-skilled immigrant workers as a result of the STEM extension program stimulates growth and innovation in start-ups and large companies alike, which in turn stimulates demand for domestic (American) high-skilled workers, as well as opportunities of local entrepreneurship. These findings disprove DHS’s argument with relation to the security and opportunity of American workers. [Source: https://bse.eu/research/working-papers/the-effect-of-retaining-high-skilled-international-graduates-evidence-from-the-stem-opt-extension]

These are just a portion of the concerns over this rule, and DHS has not done enough research into the hurt and damage that this will cause the higher education community.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and urges that it be withdrawn in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Cole Graber-Mitchell
comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposed rule because it would decrease the number of international students, decrease international students' ability to contribute to the United States, and diminish the United States' prominence as a global leader in higher education.

I am a current law student at Yale Law School. Before starting law school, I completed master's degrees as an international student from the US in the United Kingdom; before that, I got my bachelor's degree from Amherst College.

First, international students have enhanced all of these experiences. Americans learn more and better when international students are in the clasroom because international students introduce new ideas, perspectives, and approaches. Any rule change that decreases the number of international students coming to the United States, as this OPT change would, only diminishes universities' ability to educate the Americans we need to address the problems of today and tomorrow. This includes competition in science, technology, and culture on the world stage.

Second, international students, through OPT, contribute to the United States. They enhance our economy and help our businesses succeed, but they also contribute in countless other ways. They help cure diseases. They do basic scientific and mathematical research. They write and edit novels. They build computer systems and software. They design bridges. OPT allows the best of the best from around the world—international students accepted into America's world-renouned higher education system—to stay in the United States and use their abilities, skill, and knowledge to contribute this country, not another.

Finally, the United States higher educational system is truly the gem of the world. This change to OPT, by discouraging international students, would diminish this—and in so doing, reduce America's soft power. When international students come to the United States, they do not merely learn math, literature, history, or whatever they're studying. They also learn about American culture. They buy American products. They meet American friends. They develop stronger English skills. They grow to love a specific place in America, whether it's the fields of Iowa, the sprawling cities of Texas, or the conurbation of the Northeast. In short, they become, to one degree or another, partisans and ambassadors for America on the world-wide stage. By making it less desireable to study in the United States, these OPT changes would hurt our educational soft power. Squandering this resource is a massive, unforced error.

I am totally against these changes. They are cruel and short-sided. They hurt Americans and they hurt international students. Frankly, they are stupid.

The agency should not go forward these proposed rule changes.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by International Affairs Advisory Board
comments.commentText:
This is from an external advisory board and not on behalf of the University of Kansas.

Re: DHS Proposed Rule on Optional Practical Training Fees
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

To Whom It May Concern:

On behalf of the International Affairs External Advisory Board, we write to express our strong concerns regarding the Department of Homeland Security's proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

The proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT would create a significant financial barrier for international students seeking practical training in their fields of study. It would also place an extraordinary burden on universities and threaten their ability to attract talented students from around the world. We submit that the proposed fee increase is arbitrary and capricious, bears no reasonable relationship to the costs of administering OPT, serves no discernible public purpose, and would severely undermine the many benefits generated by the program.

At the University of Kansas, 418 graduates are currently participating in OPT. Applying the proposed fee to that number of students would represent more than $29 million in additional costs. Such a burden would be unsustainable for students and institutions alike.

International students make important contributions to our universities, workforce, and economy. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $230.9 million to the Kansas economy and supported 1,466 jobs in 2024. OPT provides these students with valuable professional experience while helping American employers access skilled talent, particularly in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics.

As an advisory board committed to strengthening international education and engagement, we believe the proposed fees would undermine the competitiveness of American higher education, weaken university-industry partnerships, and diminish opportunities for international collaboration.

We respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider the proposed fees and preserve meaningful access to Optional Practical Training by maintaining current fees or limiting any increases to demonstrable additional administrative costs, and ensuring that any other proposed changes serve a clearly defined public purpose.

Sincerely,

James Harder, Chair
Nicole Horton, Vice Chair

International Affairs External Advisory Board
University of Kansas
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create an unsustainable financial barrier for students and institutions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As a DSO at a SEVP-certified institution, I oppose the proposed rule and urge that the proposed rule be withdrawn in its entirety, and that the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program remains intact.

DHS states that “The OPT program instead relies heavily on DSOs, who are often overwhelmed by the program responsibilities and not fully trained, to be the initial gatekeepers for OPT authorization.” (p. 64575). It is important to note that DSOs do not have the authority to gatekeep or authorize OPT employment. DSOs issue OPT recommendation I-20s based on the eligibility requirements outlined by DHS as follows:
"- The student has been a full-time student for one academic year in an SEVP-certified: College/University/Conservatory/Seminary
- The student is not studying English as a Second Language.
- The student’s proposed employment relates to the student’s major area of study
- The student has not used all optional practical training available at the current level of study.
- The student has not been authorized for 12 months or more of full-time Curricular Practical Training (CPT)." (Study in the States)

As per 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i), it is the student's responsibility to initiate the OPT application process, and the role of the DSO in pre-completion and post-completion OPT is limited to issuing the recommendation. The primary responsibilities of a DSO for post-completion OPT are outlined in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)(A), which states that "Prior to making a recommendation, the DSO at the educational institution of the student's most recent enrollment must ensure that the student is eligible for the given type and period of OPT and that the student is aware of the student's responsibilities for maintaining status while on OPT". No other additional responsibilities are listed for DSOs for post-completion OPT, especially with respect to alleged OPT abuse or employer fraud. The final authority for granting OPT authorization lies with USCIS, and once post-completion OPT is approved, the DSO's role in maintaining compliance is to updating the student's record with any changes in personal information or employment reported by the student (8 CFR 214.2(f)(12)(i)). DSOs are involved to the extent of ensuring compliance with existing eligibility and reporting requirements laid down by SEVP and DHS; if DHS holds the opinion that the current eligibility requirements require review, it is not clear why an enormous tax on SEVP institutions and additional burden on DSOs is the logical approach here.

Given the limited role of DSOs and institutions in determining OPT eligibility, I believe the rationale for placing the burden of the “fee” and the enforcement of fee on DSOs and institutions is unfounded and should not be advanced.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed rule and urges that it be withdrawn in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed rule, Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, which would exacerbate economic inequality among international students and place undue financial pressure on students seeking to contribute their skills and knowledge to our national community. I oppose this proposal for two main reasons: first, it would prevent talented students from meaningfully contributing to the United States; and second, it would violate fundamental principles of fairness.

As a law student, I have seen firsthand the talent and dedication that international students bring to our academic community. Talented, brilliant, eager students come from other countries to pursue degrees here in the United States, and many hope to apply their education to important legal issues facing this country. The proposed fees would create an extraordinary financial barrier to that opportunity. Students unable to secure funding could lose access to practical training directly related to their degrees and, absent another lawful basis to remain, have to leave the country.

While many citizens care deeply about the issues facing our communities, international graduates can contribute additional skills, perspectives, and effort to addressing them. In the legal profession, those contributions could include helping clients navigate complex proceedings, representing people who cannot afford counsel, and advancing the fair administration of justice. Making those opportunities depend on access to substantial financial resources would exclude capable graduates whose work could benefit the people this policy is intended to protect.

The proposal could also distort students’ career choices. If students or prospective employers must ultimately bear the cost, graduates interested in public service could face particular difficulty finding a financially viable opportunity. A student’s commitment to serving vulnerable communities does not make an enormous fee easier to afford, and an organization’s need for skilled assistance does not mean it has the resources to fund that fee. The result could be to steer graduates toward the employers best able to absorb the expense, while making service-oriented work less accessible.

There is also a fundamental fairness issue at play. Students came here under the current OPT framework with a reasonable expectation that, if they satisfied the applicable requirements, they could seek practical training without this extraordinary additional expense. Many uprooted their lives, took on debt, and committed years to pursuing degrees in the United States. Applying the new fees to students already enrolled would pull the rug out from under people who made consequential decisions under substantially different financial conditions.

More broadly, the ability to finance such a fee is a poor measure of either professional promise or commitment to following the law. Students with fewer resources may be just as capable, diligent, and deserving of practical training as their wealthier peers. Legitimate concerns about fraud and program integrity should be addressed through measures directed at misconduct, with careful consideration of the burden imposed on students who comply with the rules.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. Our country benefits when students can apply their education in ways that serve our communities. This proposal would diminish those contributions while imposing a profound and unexpected burden on people who have already invested heavily in their education here.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fee rule because it creates financial barriers for international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Karuna Nandkumar
comments.commentText:
I am a student at Yale Law School, and I write to oppose DHS’s proposed rule that would charge schools $70,000 for a student’s first Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for each one after that. DHS acknowledges these costs could be passed on to students or employers. In practice, a fee this large works as a barrier to OPT itself. Its effects would reach every student at my school, not only the international students who need OPT. I ask DHS to withdraw the rule, or at minimum to explain how it weighed the harms below with the alleged benefits.

1. The rule would shrink the pool of students who choose to study in the United States.

Prospective students decide where to study based on everything a degree makes possible, including practical work experience after graduation. Attaching a $70,000 charge to that first step tells talented applicants that the U.S. is a costlier and less welcoming destination than the U.K., Canada, Australia, or elsewhere. Schools facing the fee may limit how many recommendations they make. Employers may decline candidates who come with a five-figure surcharge. Either way, many of the strongest applicants will reasonably go elsewhere.

That loss is not limited to international students. My legal education depends on the people in the room. In classes on constitutional law, international law, and comparative regulation, classmates who have lived under other legal systems sharpen discussions in ways no casebook can. For example, our moot court team last year included domestic and international students, leading us to win competitions. Fewer international students means a narrower, less rigorous classroom for all of us and a less competitive institution. American universities are regarded as the best in the world partly because they attract the best students from everywhere, and this rule erodes that advantage.

2. The rule would degrade the learning environment for students already here.

The proposal is already affecting my classmates. International students who planned their careers around OPT now face uncertainty about whether they can work after graduation at all, or whether an employer will absorb a $30,000 to $70,000 cost to hire them. I have seen classmates delaying or abandoning job searches, recruiters asking about status, and students considering leaving. Uncertainty about whether one can stay and work is a serious source of stress, and I have watched it affect peers’ ability to focus, participate, and engage. A school is a community. When a significant share of students are anxious and in a precarious position, the whole environment becomes more strained. DHS should account for these costs to students’ well-being and to the educational experience of everyone around them, American and international students.

3. The rule would weaken the U.S. talent pool and economy.

The United States has long benefited from attracting ambitious people from around the world, training them, and keeping them here to build companies, conduct research, and serve clients. OPT is a key bridge between education and that contribution. Pricing it out of reach means the U.S. will educate talented people and then send them abroad to compete against American firms. Employers would face either a new hiring tax or the loss of candidates they judged most qualified. This is self-defeating for a nation whose strength has always come in part from immigrants.

4. The rule would undermine national security, which is the core of DHS’s mission.

Economic and technological leadership is a national security asset. Fields central to security depend on recruiting top talent, including cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, and the legal and policy expertise that governs them. Driving that talent to strategic competitors strengthens them at our expense. Students who study and work here also become lasting ties to this country, carrying American legal and democratic norms into governments and businesses worldwide. OPT participants already remain within the student visa system, subject to reporting requirements. A fee does nothing to improve vetting; it only pushes talented people toward other countries. If DHS has specific security concerns about OPT, targeted screening would address them far better than a flat financial barrier.

Ultimately, the proposed fees would make American education less attractive, harm students already enrolled, weaken the domestic talent pool, and undercut national security. I urge DHS to withdraw the rule.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees act as a harmful barrier and asks DHS to withdraw the rule.

Employers that stop hiring international graduates in the U.S. do not stop needing that talent. Large companies can hire the same people in their offices in Canada, the UK, or India. When that happens, the salary, the income taxes, and the jobs connected to that role leave the United States, while the company keeps operating. Small businesses and startups cannot open offices abroad, so they simply lose access to talent their larger competitors can still reach. The rule would tilt the labor market toward the biggest firms and against new American companies.

The government would also lose its own investment. Federal research grants support the graduate programs and labs where many international students train. OPT is how that training is put to work in the U.S. economy. A charge of up to $70,000 at exactly that moment means the United States helps develop this talent and then makes it too expensive to keep.

Harm to education.
OPT is practical training directly related to a student's field of study. It is part of the F-1 educational program, not a separate benefit. A fee on the school's recommendation is a fee on completing that education. Programs built around practical training, and the employer partnerships that support them, would lose much of their value. Prospective students compare what a degree leads to. A U.S. degree that can no longer lead to U.S. work experience will lose applicants to countries that still offer it.

Long-term harm.
Hiring policies are sticky. Once a company removes OPT hiring from its recruiting rules, campus pipelines close and recruiters stop coming. Even if this rule is later reversed, those decisions are rarely revisited quickly. The 294,253 students on OPT in 2024-25 (Open Doors 2025) are also the alumni that future applicants ask whether studying in the U.S. is worth it. This rule would give them a clear answer: no.

Requests to DHS.
I ask DHS to withdraw the rule. If DHS proceeds, it must:
(a) analyze how much of the fee will be passed to employers and how many employers will stop hiring OPT students as a result;
(b) assess the impact on small businesses and startups compared with large firms;
(c) estimate how many positions would move offshore and the resulting loss of federal and state tax revenue; and
(d) explain why those costs are justified by fraud deterrence when DHS already has targeted enforcement tools.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states strong opposition to the proposed OPT fee rule and urges DHS to withdraw it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Lindsay Poland
comments.commentText:
The proposed fee is so high that it would be a de facto end to OPT for most students. I work at a community college where most of our students earn Certificates and Associate degrees. Students with Associate degrees in the U.S. make an average salary of about $50,000 - $55,000 (https://www.bls.gov/careeroutlook/2018/article/postsecondary-outlook.htm). The new proposed fee of $70,000 to apply for OPT would be asking students to pay more than twice the amount that they need to show they have available for one academic year on their I-20, and would be impossible for most of our students.
In addition, many of our students applying for OPT are looking for entry-level jobs or internships in business, education, nursing, or computer science. The vast majority of them could never hope to make $70,000 in their single year of OPT even IF USCIS manages to process their applications fast enough for them to get the whole 12 months (the current estimated time for 80% of applications is 5 months if students don't pay the $1,780 "Premium Processing Fee" to push their application to the front of the line, which most of our students cannot do), and if they can overcome all of the other hurdles international students face with applying for SSNs, divers licenses, and explaining how OPT/work authorization works to employers. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Laura Flower Kim
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I am writing in strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and an additional $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations.

I have worked in international higher education for nearly two decades and currently work at a top-tier STEM institution on the West Coast. I have worked closely with international students who come to the United States to pursue an exceptional education and contribute their knowledge, skills, and talents to our country.

These fees are outrageous and would make OPT financially inaccessible to most international students. Few institutions could absorb such costs for each eligible student. Shifting the burden to students or employers does not solve the problem. Students cannot afford an additional $70,000 to $100,000 for practical training, and employers are unlikely to pay such amounts to hire recent graduates.

Consider a student seeking just three months of summer internship experience through pre-completion OPT. Under this proposal, the student's school would face a $70,000 fee to recommend that training, potentially followed by another $30,000 for post-completion OPT. Institutions would have little choice but to stop recommending otherwise eligible students. What educational purpose does that serve?

The consequences would begin long before graduation. International students invest significantly in a U.S. education, often expecting the opportunity to apply what they have learned through practical training. If that opportunity becomes financially unattainable, why would they choose the United States over countries offering excellent education and more accessible post-study opportunities? A 2025 IDP Education survey found that 66% of respondents would choose or consider another destination if post-graduation work opportunities were unavailable.

I am especially concerned about American competitiveness in STEM. Our universities educate some of the world's most talented students and researchers. They contribute to research, innovation, entrepreneurship, and the advancement of knowledge. Many continue contributing to American industry and academia after graduation. We would effectively be educating talented individuals in the United States and then encouraging them to take their knowledge, skills, and entrepreneurial potential to other countries. That makes little sense when countries are actively competing for the same talent.

American students and workers would also feel the effects. International student tuition supports academic programs, faculty positions, research, and opportunities for domestic students. Research cited by NAFSA from the Institute for Progress projects that the proposed fees could ultimately result in approximately 46,000 fewer American students enrolling annually in bachelor's and master's programs. While this is an estimate, it underscores how a policy intended to protect American workers could instead harm American educational opportunities.

I also question how these fees would address fraud. OPT already operates under federal oversight. STEM OPT includes E-Verify participation, formal training plans, evaluations, and reporting requirements. DHS has tools to investigate noncompliance. Imposing extraordinary charges on every participating school and student, regardless of compliance history, is not a targeted response. Nor has DHS adequately shown how a $70,000 charge for an OPT recommendation relates to the actual cost of administering or enforcing the program.

OPT connects American education with practical experience and helps international alumni contribute to our economy, industry, and academia. Rather than drive away the talent our universities have educated, DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue reasonable, targeted approaches to program integrity.

I submit this comment in my individual capacity, based on my professional experience and personal perspective.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed exorbitant OPT fees, arguing they make the program financially inaccessible.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a first-year student at Yale Law School and an Army veteran. I write to oppose the proposed rule requiring a $70,000 fee for a student’s first Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for each later one, including the STEM OPT extension. DHS should withdraw it.
The fee has no connection to any cost DHS incurs. Federal user fees must be fair and based on the government’s costs and the value of the service (31 U.S.C. § 9701). Students now pay roughly $500 to apply for OPT work authorization. The rule raises that by about 13,900 percent without identifying any new adjudication or oversight cost a $70,000 charge would cover. A charge set far above cost and deposited into the general treasury is not a user fee. It is a tax, and only Congress may levy taxes.
DHS lacks the authority it claims. The rule rests on DHS’s general power to set “conditions” on nonimmigrant status. That provision is not a grant of power to impose a five-figure charge whose evident purpose is to make a lawful, decades-old program unaffordable. After Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024), DHS receives no deference on its reading of its own statutory authority, and courts have already rejected a comparable theory used to justify the $100,000 H-1B fee. Congress, not an agency, decides whether to restrict post-study work.
The rule ignores serious reliance interests. Hundreds of thousands of students chose U.S. schools, paid tuition, and often took on debt with the reasonable expectation that OPT would be available on the terms that have existed for years. DHS v. Regents (2020) requires an agency changing course to weigh such reliance. The proposed grandfathering is largely illusory: because the $30,000 fee applies only where the $70,000 fee was already paid, a student already on OPT who seeks a STEM extension after the effective date would owe the full $70,000.
The cost will fall on those least able to bear it. Schools pay the fee, but the rule lets them pass it to students or employers. Wealthy universities may absorb some of it; community colleges, regional public universities, and smaller schools cannot. Startups and small businesses cannot pay $70,000 to hire a recent graduate. The practical result is that OPT becomes available only to the wealthiest students and largest employers, rewarding family resources rather than talent and effort, and forcing schools to decide which students are “worth” the fee.
The rule harms American competitiveness. Nearly 300,000 international students participate in OPT each year (Open Doors). Many work in science, engineering, medicine, and research, often in fields with persistent shortages, and many go on to found companies that employ Americans. Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Germany all offer post-study work options and actively recruit these graduates. A $70,000 barrier hands that talent to our competitors. As someone who has served in uniform, I understand that national security depends on economic and technological strength; driving away people the United States has spent years educating weakens both.
DHS’s stated concerns call for targeted tools, not a blanket fee. DHS asserts that OPT should not be a “back door” into the workforce or a subsidy for cheap labor. If there is abuse, DHS already has SEVP oversight, employer reporting requirements, the STEM OPT training plan and wage protections, and its enforcement powers. It can strengthen those. A uniform $70,000 charge does not distinguish fraud from legitimate training; it simply prices out everyone who cannot pay, including the students who follow every rule. The rule also does not show that OPT participants depress U.S. wages, and the existing STEM OPT rule already requires wages commensurate with those of similarly situated U.S. workers.
The comment period is inadequate. A 30-day window is too short for a rule with consequences this large for universities, employers, and students across the country, many of whom are only now learning of it.
The proposed fees are unlawful, unsupported by any cost analysis, and harmful to students, schools, employers, and the national interest. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.

I am writing to oppose DHS's proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. These fees risk weakening America's economic competitiveness, technological leadership, and national interests.

I currently work as a research associate at a U.S. university, using data science and computational methods to support academic research. I am also preparing to pursue a PhD in the United States. I have seen how OPT enables international graduates to contribute to U.S. research and the economy.

Artificial intelligence and advanced computing are increasingly central to economic growth and national security. America's leadership requires both investment and skilled researchers.

The United States already has an enormous competitive advantage: its universities attract talented students from around the world. According to the National Science Foundation's Science & Engineering Indicators 2026, temporary visa holders earned 61% of U.S. computer and information sciences doctorates and 54% of engineering doctorates in 2024. International talent is deeply integrated into America's advanced research workforce.

A $70,000 fee would make many legitimate research appointments financially impractical. Predoctoral research associates often work with professors on data analysis, software development, and empirical studies. These positions are essential to academic productivity but frequently operate on limited university research budgets. In some cases, the proposed fee could approach or exceed an entire year's salary.

I am especially concerned about the implications for AI. As AI transforms the economy, the United States needs researchers who combine computational expertise with knowledge of economics, business, engineering, and other disciplines. OPT helps connect the education provided by American universities with the research and innovation taking place here.

The proposed fees could weaken this connection. Students may become less willing to invest years studying in the United States if practical training becomes financially inaccessible. Universities may become less willing to recruit them. Graduates who could contribute to American research and industry may instead pursue opportunities abroad.

I recognize DHS's responsibility to prevent fraud and protect American workers. I support those goals. Employers that abuse OPT should face meaningful penalties, and practical training should involve genuine work and appropriate compensation.

However, imposing extraordinary fees on legitimate training opportunities is not a targeted response to fraud. A university employing a researcher on a genuine academic project should not face a prohibitive financial barrier because unrelated employers may misuse the program.

More effective alternatives include risk-based employer audits, stronger verification of training arrangements, enforcement of existing compensation requirements, and penalties directed at demonstrated violations.

I also urge DHS to more carefully evaluate the proposal's economic consequences. The regulatory analysis acknowledges uncertainty about how much OPT participation would decline. Before adopting fees of this magnitude, DHS should examine the potential effects on university research employment, doctoral recruitment, innovation, and the retention of highly trained graduates.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and pursue proportionate, evidence-based measures that address genuine abuses without undermining America's research workforce.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposal describes alleged misconduct involving false employment letters, shell companies, staged worksites, improper placement arrangements, and misrepresentations by employers or students. These concerns merit investigation. But the fee would be imposed on schools when they recommend students, regardless of whether the student later obtains legitimate employment or fraud is found. Schools generally do not control employers’ operations, worksites, payroll, wages, or tax compliance, and cannot compel employers to provide business records. DHS notes that OPT and STEM OPT employers generally are not required to submit supporting documents, such as tax records or proof of business, and that employer attestations are not generally verified unless a site visit occurs. See Proposed Rule, 91 FR 64573. That supports improving employer verification—not making schools financially responsible for information they cannot obtain.

DHS should focus on the parties and conduct that present risk. Options include requiring relevant employer records, verifying information against available data, conducting targeted site visits, and investigating suspected shell companies and false submissions. A school’s payment of a fee cannot ensure employer compliance or prevent a student from providing false information. Schools cannot reliably assess whether a student is a “strong candidate”

The proposed rule calls DSOs “initial gatekeepers” and suggests schools may decline to recommend students they do not consider a “strong candidate” for OPT. Proposed Rule, 91 FR 64578. It does not define that standard or explain what evidence schools should use to apply it consistently and fairly. When making a recommendation, a DSO may not know the student’s future employer, worksite, duties, or the employer’s compliance history. DSOs confirm applicable requirements and maintain SEVIS information; they do not adjudicate Form I-765 applications, investigate employers, or inspect worksites. A DSO signing Form I-20 certifies under penalty of perjury that the information provided is true and correct. That should not make schools responsible for facts outside their knowledge or control. The Department describes SEVIS-USCIS data errors, correction requests, and communication problems that consume DSO time. DHS should address these capacity and information gaps before asking DSOs to make more consequential judgments.

DHS says the fee would reduce or stabilize participation and lessen enforcement burdens. Proposed Rule, 91 FR 64574–75. But reducing participation does not necessarily improve compliance; a fee may deter compliant students and employers without resolving verification problems. DHS considered broader reporting requirements, including approaches used for STEM OPT, but favored a fee partly because it could be implemented more quickly and require less government administration. Id. at 64576.

DHS should instead:

Use employer records and existing information. Require documentation calibrated to risk, such as evidence of business operations, registration, worksites, payroll, or supervision. Form I-983 records STEM OPT employment and training details and is retained by the DSO. DHS should assess requiring it to be uploaded when STEM OPT is recommended; it is currently optional.

Target investigations. Prioritize site visits and investigations using indicators such as unverifiable addresses, unusually high concentrations of OPT workers, inconsistent information, third-party placement arrangements, or prior compliance findings. DHS should assess whether SEVIS can identify patterns linking students to employers of concern and improve the system if needed.

Improve data and communication. DHS identifies SEVIS-USCIS data and communication problems, including issues involving the Computer-Linked Application Information Management System (CLAIMS). More accurate, timely data and clear channels for resolving discrepancies would improve oversight and reduce the burden on schools.

Use existing tools and build agency capacity. SEVP has described the ability to terminate SEVIS records when students exceed unemployment limits—90 days for post-completion OPT and 150 days for STEM OPT. I am not aware of this mechanism being applied at scale. DHS should explain how it is used and what limits its implementation. GAO-19-297 recommended that ICE evaluate recertification resources and develop fraud-specific DSO training; ICE concurred. DHS should invest in agency capacity and training rather than shift enforcement costs to schools through a $70,000 fee.

I support effective action against OPT fraud and abuse. The proposed fee is not tailored to misconduct and gives schools no means to verify employer operations. I urge DHS to withdraw it and pursue targeted employer oversight, improved agency systems, and adequate staffing and training.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule "Optional Practical Training Fees" (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, 91 FR 64566) and urge DHS to withdraw it in its entirety. It would undercut the federal government's own fiscal and strategic interests, damage American higher education, and cause long-term harm to U.S. competitiveness that a later repeal could not easily undo.

1. The rule works against the U.S. government's own interests.
DHS estimates the fees at $8.4 to $16.5 billion per year across 2,478 schools. That number measures a burden, not revenue. Few schools can pay $70,000 per student, so the likely result is fewer OPT recommendations, not more money. Meanwhile, the government would lose what OPT already produces. International students contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs in 2024-25 (NAFSA), and 294,253 of them were on OPT (Open Doors 2025). OPT participants earn U.S. wages, pay federal and state income taxes, and spend in local economies. Driving them away shrinks the tax base. The $30,000 charge on STEM OPT extensions falls on exactly the graduates in AI, semiconductors, and engineering that U.S. industry and national security depend on.

DHS says the fee would offset administrative costs, yet students already pay USCIS a separate filing fee for OPT work authorization, and nothing suggests that a school's recommendation costs anywhere near $70,000 to oversee. A charge this large, deposited into the general Treasury and untethered from the cost of any service, functions as a tax. DHS has not shown that its authority to set "conditions" on nonimmigrant status allows it to impose one. Finalizing the rule would invite litigation and years of uncertainty at taxpayer expense. If the goal is fraud prevention, a flat charge on every compliant student is the wrong tool. DHS already has SEVIS reporting, STEM OPT training plans, and site visits to target actual violations.

2. The rule would damage American education.
Schools would face three choices: absorb $70,000 per student, pass the cost to students, or stop recommending OPT. The first is impossible for most institutions. The second prices out all but the wealthiest students. The third ends OPT in practice. Designated School Officials would become gatekeepers deciding whose careers the school can afford, a role the regulations never gave them.

International tuition helps fund financial aid for domestic students, faculty positions, graduate programs, and research labs. NAFSA and JB International already project a $3.4 billion loss and nearly 40,000 jobs from Fall 2026 enrollment declines, driven mainly by graduate students. This rule would accelerate that decline. Small colleges, community colleges, and regional public universities, many of them small entities under the Regulatory Flexibility Act, would be hit hardest.

3. The damage would last.
Students choose a country years before they graduate, and their experience shapes where the next class applies. A $70,000 price on post-graduation training tells the world's best students that the United States does not want them. Countries with post-study work pathways, such as the UK, Canada, and Australia, will take that talent. A quarter of America's billion-dollar startups had a founder who first came to the U.S. as an international student (NFAP, 2022), and those companies employ Americans. Once that pipeline moves elsewhere, it will not come back simply because the rule is later reversed.

4. How it affects me.
I am an international graduate student on an F-1 visa. OPT is the bridge between my U.S. education and contributing to a U.S. employer. Under this rule, whether I can work would depend not on my qualifications or an employer's need, but on whether my school is willing to pay $70,000 on my behalf.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. At a minimum, before any final rule, DHS must:
(a) explain how the $70,000 and $30,000 amounts were calculated and how they relate to actual program costs;
(b) identify specific statutory authority for a fee deposited into the general Treasury;
(c) quantify lost federal and state tax revenue and economic activity;
(d) complete a full Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis for small institutions; and
(e) explain why targeted enforcement is not a less harmful alternative.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Carolina Lawrence
comments.commentText:
I am an international graduate student currently pursuing my master's degree in the United States. I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule, "Optional Practical Training Fees," particularly the proposed fee requirements under 8 CFR 214.13(i).

Like many international students, I chose to study in the United States because of its outstanding educational opportunities, innovative environment, and the possibility of gaining practical experience related to my field of study. Pursuing graduate education here requires a significant investment of time, money, and effort. Optional Practical Training (OPT) is an important part of that educational journey because it allows students to apply their academic knowledge in real-world professional settings.

**First, the proposed fees would create unreasonable financial barriers.** Requiring educational institutions to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions, could make it financially impossible for many universities to support their international students. Although these fees would formally be paid by institutions, students could ultimately bear the consequences through reduced OPT opportunities, additional financial pressure, or the inability to obtain school recommendations.

**Second, the proposal would undermine the value of American higher education.** International students contribute substantial tuition revenue, diverse perspectives, and academic talent to American universities. Practical training is often a major consideration when students decide where to pursue higher education. If OPT becomes inaccessible, future international students may choose to study in other countries, weakening the United States' ability to attract and retain global talent.

**Third, the proposed rule could negatively affect American businesses and innovation.** International graduates bring specialized knowledge, technical skills, and diverse perspectives to the workforce. Preventing qualified graduates from gaining practical experience could deprive American employers of valuable talent and reduce opportunities for collaboration and innovation.

I recognize the government's responsibility to prevent immigration fraud and protect American workers. However, imposing extraordinarily high fees on educational institutions is not a reasonable or proportionate solution. Stronger compliance monitoring, targeted investigations, and enforcement against actual violations would be more appropriate alternatives.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fee requirements and preserve meaningful access to practical training for qualified international students.

International students come to the United States not only to receive an education, but also to develop skills, contribute to their communities, and participate in the country's academic and economic success. Policies should encourage these positive contributions rather than create unnecessary barriers.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they create unreasonable financial barriers for students and institutions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Dylan Carter
comments.commentText:
This rule to put a fee on OPT recommendations is a gross expression of xenophobia. This change and the levying of fees on institutions will make these important work opportunities less accessible for talented students across the country. Such a steep fee will severely restrict this opportunity to many students who deserve to continue the work they have started as a student.

I also would like to take a second to speak on the use of citations. Please don't bother with a citation if the citation is simply a link to a DHS press conference on YouTube (citation 55). International students work incredibly hard and take significant risk to study at institutions in the US. It is not an easy feat to make the commitment to travel so far for so long and they deserve to be treated respect and dignity. This is a plain attack against all international students which punishes and demonizes them with no merit to its justification.

This rule should NOT be implemented.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Asian Rehabilitation Counseling Society
comments.commentText:
The Asian Rehabilitation Counseling Society (ARCS) respectfully opposes the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and the additional $30,000 fee for subsequent participation.

Rehabilitation counseling plays a critical role in promoting employment, independence, community participation, and quality of life for individuals with disabilities. Preparing qualified rehabilitation counselors requires specialized graduate education, supervised clinical experiences, and opportunities to apply professional knowledge and skills in real-world settings. OPT provides an important pathway for international graduates of rehabilitation counseling and related programs to gain practical experience, develop professional competencies, and contribute to the U.S. workforce.

The proposed fees would create substantial financial barriers for international graduates and prospective employers, including rehabilitation agencies, community-based organizations, healthcare institutions, and educational settings. These financial burdens could discourage employers from hiring qualified international professionals, restrict access to employment opportunities, and undermine efforts to address workforce needs in rehabilitation counseling and disability services.

The consequences extend beyond individual graduates. International rehabilitation counseling professionals contribute valuable linguistic, cultural, and professional perspectives that strengthen culturally responsive counseling, vocational rehabilitation, disability advocacy, and research. Their contributions are particularly important in serving individuals with disabilities from diverse racial, ethnic, linguistic, and immigrant communities who may already experience significant barriers to accessing rehabilitation and employment services.

ARCS is committed to advancing diversity, equity, inclusion, and culturally responsive practices within rehabilitation counseling. Policies that impose prohibitive financial barriers on international professionals risk weakening the rehabilitation workforce, reducing diversity within the profession, and limiting access to quality services for individuals with disabilities.

We urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to reconsider the proposed fee structure, provide a transparent and evidence-based justification for the proposed amounts, and explore less burdensome alternatives that maintain appropriate oversight while preserving equitable pathways to professional training and employment in rehabilitation counseling.

Best regards,

Jinhee Park
President of the Asian Rehabilitation Counseling Society
