comments.title: Comment Submitted by Geneva College
comments.commentText: Geneva College is a small institution with approximately 1,100 undergraduates and 100 graduates. Of these, our F-1 student population numbers about 35. As a small Christian institution, we have some concerns about the recent proposed rule concerning the new fees for Optional Practical Training. Each year, we have between 5 and 7 students who apply for OPT. The proposed rule states, on page 64574 under section C, that “By establishing a financial obligation through a fee, this proposed rule would encourage schools to ensure that OPT opportunities provide genuine educational value that aligns with the original intent of the practical training program, thereby promoting shared responsibility and accountability.” We do our best to ensure that our students are moving into positions that are supplying this educational value, and our students appreciate the opportunities that OPT offers. For example, this past year, we had a student who graduated with his bachelor's degree in May. He worked for a company through the end of October, gaining experience in the chemical engineering field before moving to Amsterdam, Netherlands to pursue a graduate degree. Two years ago, one of our students graduated with a degree in Business and worked for a company here in the US during his year of OPT. He has now started his own business in São Paulo, Brazil. In 2023, one of our undergraduate students graduated with a degree in engineering and proceeded to complete her year of OPT and then pursued her STEM OPT. She was later accepted for an H1-B visa. Our students who pursue OPT find the experience invaluable to their future endeavors whether it be moving onto a graduate school or pursuing work in their home country and abroad. Many of our students consider OPT to be a benefit of coming to the States for higher education. Their experience in the US workforce expands their resume and makes them competitive candidates for jobs and graduate programs. As a small institution, Geneva College cannot afford to spend $70,000 for each student who has a desire to pursue their optional practical training, and thus, would not be able to offer this as an option for F-1 students. We realize that we operate on a dramatically smaller scale in comparison to other universities. However, we value our international students and the unique perspectives that they bring to our campus and our community. Currently, about 90% of our F-1 students are involved in student leadership.  They serve as resident assistants, on our Dean's council, as club leaders, and participate in our Honors Program. They are active participants in our student body and become active participants in our community as they graduate and seek OPT opportunities in the greater Pittsburgh area in fields like education, nursing, and engineering. Over the 2024-25 academic year, “international student enrollment contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy” (NAFSA). It is also important to note that 48% of our F-1 students are currently pursuing a STEM field of study. According to NASFA: Association of International Educators, “more than half of international students in the United States pursue STEM fields of study and 70% of full‑time graduate students in AI-related fields are international students.” It feels especially important now, as AI and other technology rapidly develops, that we attract these students to pursue education in the United States and offer them additional opportunities, such as OPT, in order to meet the demands of our 21st century knowledge economy.  We benefit as much as our students do, through both their financial and knowledge contributions. Most institutions will not be able to pay the proposed OPT fee, and according to a survey conducted by Inside Higher Education, over 50% of F-1 students attend school in the United States with intentions of pursuing OPT. Without this opportunity, international students may take their financial and knowledge contributions to other countries. If the United States wants to remain great, then we need to continue to attract great minds from across the globe.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. I urge DHS to withdraw this fee structure and preserve reasonable access to legitimate, degree-related practical training.

My principal concern is that these fees would make access to practical training depend on financial resources rather than educational merit, professional qualifications, or compliance with immigration requirements. Although the proposal places payment responsibility on educational institutions, it acknowledges that those institutions may pass the financial burden to students or employers. Shifting responsibility for payment does not eliminate the burden. I am concerned that institutions could decline to recommend otherwise qualified students, employers could withdraw legitimate training opportunities, and students could lose access to practical experience despite meeting all other eligibility requirements.

I support protecting American workers, preventing fraud, and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, the ability to pay a substantial fee is not evidence of compliance, and the inability to pay is not evidence of misconduct. DHS should demonstrate why these particular amounts would effectively distinguish legitimate educational training from abuse. A reduction in participation should not, by itself, be treated as evidence that fraud has been prevented.

The proposal states that the fees would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury and would not be retained by ICE or specifically earmarked for immigration enforcement activities. I therefore ask DHS to explain how these fees would improve oversight beyond creating a financial deterrent. The agency should evaluate less burdensome alternatives, including targeted compliance reviews, verification of degree-related training, employer accountability, and enforcement of applicable worker protections. Measures directed at demonstrated misconduct would be preferable to a financial barrier affecting compliant participants.

I am also concerned about the proposed effective date of 60 days after publication of a final rule. DHS should meaningfully consider students who have already committed to educational programs, incurred substantial expenses, or accepted future training opportunities under the existing framework. Describing a requirement as prospective does not resolve its potential impact on decisions made years earlier. I request explicit protections for currently enrolled students and existing OPT participants, including those who would need a later recommendation or extension.

Before proceeding, DHS should assess the potential consequences for universities, teaching hospitals, veterinary services, scientific research, small employers, and underserved communities. The analysis should examine whether these fees could discourage legitimate clinical training, interrupt research, reduce educational opportunities, or limit access to essential services. It should also consider whether smaller institutions and modestly funded training programs would face disproportionate barriers compared with organizations possessing greater financial resources.

DHS should also evaluate whether shifting substantial costs to students could increase debt or dependence on employers willing to finance participation. A policy intended to protect workers should be examined carefully for the possibility that it could make participants more financially vulnerable.

For these reasons, I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee structure. Any alternative should be supported by transparent evidence, proportionate to its stated objectives, and designed to address demonstrated problems without making legitimate training financially unattainable. At a minimum, DHS should evaluate substantially lower fees, meaningful exemptions or waivers, and transition protections for students with existing educational commitments.

Protecting American workers and preserving immigration integrity are important goals. They should be pursued through effective oversight and evidence-based enforcement, not by making lawful, education-related practical training accessible only to those with exceptional financial resources.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the fee structure.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by University of Central Arkansas
comments.commentText:
Comments regarding proposed Department of Homeland Security OPT fee: 8 CFR Part 214; [DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100]; RIN 1653-AB01
November 5, 2026
The Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule No. ICEB-2026-0100 would require the University of Central Arkansas (UCA) to pay a $70,000 fee for each F-1 student approved by a Designated School Official (DSO) to apply for Optional Practical Training (OPT). Over the past five years, 44% (215) of the 494 international students who graduated from UCA were approved for OPT. If these previous approvals had been subject to the proposed $70,000 fee, the total cost would have been $15,050,000, averaging approximately $3 million annually.
While the proposed rule states that the fee may be distributed "to F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers," shifting this cost to UCA’s F-1 students would require them to secure an additional $70,000 beyond the estimated $100,000 required for four years of undergraduate study. Data from a recent Institute for Progress survey indicates that 69% of surveyed international students would not have enrolled in a U.S. program if a $70,000 fee for 12-month OPT were required. This cost projection represents an approximate 70% increase in the total cost of attendance for an undergraduate degree and subsequent OPT experience, which may lead prospective students to consider competing destinations such as the UK, Australia, or Canada, where post-graduation work permit fees are significantly lower (totaling approximately $255 in Canada). Edufabtech
International students contributed an estimated $11 million in economic value to UCA during the 2024–25 academic year, supporting 83 jobs (NAFSA). In the context of declining domestic student enrollment affecting many universities across Arkansas and the United States, the proposed fee could impact the financial accessibility of U.S. higher education for international students who choose regional institutions primarily due to competitive costs of attendance.
A decline in international enrollment also impacts campus demographics and educational environments. For domestic students preparing for global markets, cross-cultural collaboration on campus provides critical exposure. Given that less than 2% of the domestic student population at UCA studies abroad, international classmates represent an important avenue for cross-cultural exchange and diverse academic perspectives inside the classroom.
Finally, the proposed rule does not present extensive evidence of widespread fraud within the nationwide OPT framework to justify the scale of the fee. In the absence of such evidence, the proposed fee structure acts as a substantial financial barrier that would likely restrict access to post-graduation training and lower international student enrollment at institutions like the University of Central Arkansas.
Phillip Bailey,
Associate Vice-President for Global Learning and Engagement
Center for Global Learning and Engagement
University of Central Arkansas
Phillipb@uca.edu

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule "Optional Practical Training Fees" (FR Doc. 2026-20660). DHS's statement that the rule would not affect health or safety.

1. The health and safety finding has no analysis behind it
The NPRM says the rule "exceeds the $100 million expenditure threshold in the first year" and provides a UMRA statement. UMRA section 202(a)(2) requires that statement to assess the mandate's effect on health and safety. The NPRM's answer is one sentence: "DHS does not believe that this rule would have impacts on health or safety." DHS gives no data, no reasoning, and no sign that it asked the Department of Health and Human Services.

2. DHS's own scenario removes OPT for most health graduates
In its low participation scenario, DHS assumes schools will pay the $70,000 fee "for only F-1 nonimmigrant students eligible for the 24-month STEM OPT extension," and that "non-STEM OPT is no longer recommended." The STEM definition in footnote 49 covers the CIP two-digit series for engineering, biological sciences, mathematics and physical sciences, "or a related field." Most health professions degrees, including nursing and pharmacy practice degrees, sit in a different series (CIP 51) and are not on the STEM list. In that scenario, international graduates of those programs lose post-completion OPT. That is a direct effect on the health workforce, and the NPRM does not mention it.

3. The labor evidence is about computer jobs
The NPRM's labor-market case rests on computer occupations. The proclamation DHS quotes says computer science unemployment is "more than double the unemployment rates of recent biology and art history graduates." DHS cites nothing showing that OPT workers in nursing, pharmacy, public health or clinical research displace U.S. workers or depress wages. It also assumes "employers may find alternative workers." For clinical roles, that is a factual question about staffing, and DHS did not ask it. Where a hospital or clinic cannot fill a licensed position, the cost is measured in patient access, not only in payroll.

4. The refund rule fits licensed fields badly
Many health occupations require a state license, and graduates often sit for the licensing exam after the program ends. Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1), the $70,000 fee "will not be refunded under any circumstances once the F-1 student has been granted the employment authorization document." If a graduate's license is delayed, the school loses the full fee even though no patient care was ever provided. A school pricing that risk will drop health students first. DHS did not consider this.

5. Biomedical research takes the STEM path, at full price
Biological sciences graduates do qualify for STEM OPT. That means $70,000 plus $30,000 for each graduate who moves into biotech, drug development, biostatistics or clinical trial work. The NPRM names "technology and critical infrastructure" as the high-risk sectors where abuse is "more likely." It cites no OPT fraud case in biomedical research or patient care. A flat fee charges these fields the same as the sectors DHS says concern it.

6. What DHS should have done
DHS has SEVIS data by program and employer. It could have reported how many OPT and STEM OPT participants hold health professions or biomedical degrees, and how many work for hospitals, clinics, health systems or clinical research sites. It could also have checked whether those employers sit in federally designated Health Professional Shortage Areas. It did none of this before concluding there is no health effect.

7. Requests
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS re-proposes any OPT fee, it should:
(a) complete the UMRA section 202(a)(2) health and safety assessment, in consultation with HHS, and publish it for comment;
(b) publish SEVIS counts of OPT and STEM OPT participants by CIP series and by health care employer type;
(c) exempt graduates of health professions programs and OPT employment with licensed health care providers, or at minimum allow a refund when a required license is not issued; and
(d) explain why a flat fee is needed in fields where DHS cites no fraud and no labor surplus.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule, citing a lack of health and safety analysis and workforce impacts.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, Optional Practical Training Fees

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, and I urge DHS to withdraw the rule.

I am an F-1 student in an Electrical Construction Technology program at a public community college in Los Angeles. I expect to finish my program in 2027, and I have planned my studies around one year of post-completion OPT so I can work as an electrical technician. My coursework is hands-on: motor controls, control panels, transformers, VFDs, and industrial wiring. OPT is the step where that training turns into real field experience.

1. The fee would end OPT at community colleges. The rule makes the school pay before a DSO can recommend a student. A public community college that serves working-class students cannot pay $70,000 per student. In practice my college would recommend no one, and every F-1 student in a trades program would lose OPT, whatever their record. DHS does not analyze this effect on community colleges or vocational programs.

2. A price is not a fraud screen. The fee sorts students by their school's budget, not by honesty or merit. I have followed every F-1 rule. Under this proposal my OPT would depend on whether my college can find $70,000, not on anything I did. If fraud is the concern, DHS already has targeted tools: SEVIS reporting, employer verification, and enforcement against bad actors.

3. It works against U.S. workforce needs. Employers across the country report shortages of electricians and skilled technicians, and the build-out of power, solar, and industrial infrastructure needs more of them. Trades OPT is short, and students like me fill hands-on roles for a limited time. Blocking it does not protect U.S. workers. It removes trained people from jobs that are already hard to fill.

4. It is a tax, not a fee. The money goes to the Treasury rather than paying for any OPT service or oversight, and the amount bears no relation to the cost of processing a recommendation.

5. The comment period is too short. Thirty days is not enough time for students, schools, and employers to assess a rule with effects this large.

At a minimum, DHS should exempt community colleges and vocational programs, scale any fee to the actual cost of administering OPT, and keep current students under the rules they enrolled under.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fee and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:
I am writing as a PhD student at Yale University studying microbiology to express my opposition to the proposed rule under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, concerning fees associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT). I urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety. Although I am not an international student myself, I work closely with many international members of the scientific community, and their contributions are essential to my research, my laboratory, and my development as a scientist. I believe this proposal would have consequences that extend far beyond the international students directly affected. It would change the environment in which American graduate students are trained, make it harder for universities to retain talented researchers, and potentially weaken the United States' position as a global leader in scientific research.
As a microbiology PhD student, I understand that research is rarely an individual effort. Much of what we accomplish depends on the knowledge, technical skills, and perspectives of the people around us. In my laboratory, I work with international researchers who bring different academic backgrounds, specialized expertise, and valuable scientific perspectives. They contribute to experimental design, troubleshoot difficult experiments, share protocols, discuss unexpected results, and help one another develop new approaches to scientific questions. These interactions are not incidental to our work; they are fundamental to how research progresses. In microbiology, experiments can be technically demanding and time-consuming, and the ability to learn from someone with experience in a particular method or biological system can make a substantial difference to the progress of a project. Losing a trained laboratory member is not simply a matter of replacing one employee with another. It can mean losing years of accumulated knowledge, disrupting ongoing experiments, delaying publications, and forcing other members of the laboratory to spend significant time rebuilding expertise that was already present.
The proposed rule is particularly concerning because of the financial barriers it would introduce. Specifically, Section V.A. of the proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566, 64576–64577 (Oct. 8, 2026), establishes a proposed $70,000 fee for an institution's initial OPT recommendation for an F-1 student and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations under the specified conditions. The proposed regulatory provisions are 8 C.F.R. §§ 214.2(f)(11) and 214.13(i). These amounts are extraordinarily high in the context of academic research, where laboratories operate under limited grant funding and carefully planned budgets. Universities must already balance the costs of personnel, equipment, reagents, facilities, and research infrastructure. An additional financial burden of this magnitude could influence whether an institution is willing or able to support an otherwise qualified international researcher. Even if a university wants to retain a student who has spent several years contributing to its research program, the financial implications could make that decision considerably more difficult. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Yun-De Liu
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation.

I am an international graduate student pursuing an advanced degree in a STEM field at a U.S. university. My academic and professional experiences have shown me the importance of practical training opportunities in connecting higher education with industry innovation. I chose to pursue graduate education in the United States because of its world-class academic environment, research opportunities, and commitment to technological advancement.

I recognize the importance of preventing immigration fraud, protecting American workers, and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, I am deeply concerned that the proposed fees would impose disproportionate burdens on legitimate students, educational institutions, and employers without adequately distinguishing lawful participation from fraudulent activity.

First, the proposed fees would undermine the accessibility and educational purpose of OPT.

Practical training is an important extension of academic education, enabling students to apply specialized knowledge in real-world settings. A $70,000 initial fee could make such opportunities financially inaccessible, regardless of a student's academic qualifications, professional potential, or compliance with immigration requirements. This financial barrier would disproportionately affect students with limited financial resources and could discourage talented individuals from pursuing advanced education in the United States.

Second, the proposed rule could weaken American technological competitiveness and innovation.

International graduates contribute specialized knowledge and skills to American research institutions and companies working in artificial intelligence, advanced computing, semiconductor technologies, and other strategically important industries. Practical training opportunities allow American employers to benefit from talent educated within the United States. Imposing substantial financial barriers could encourage highly skilled graduates to pursue opportunities in other countries, potentially reducing America's ability to attract and retain international talent and weakening its long-term leadership in science and technology.

Third, placing the payment obligation on universities does not eliminate the financial burden on students and employers.

Although the proposed rule formally assigns payment responsibility to educational institutions, it explicitly allows institutions to pass these costs on to students or employers. Universities may also choose not to recommend otherwise qualified students because of the substantial financial obligation. Consequently, access to practical training could become increasingly dependent on financial resources rather than academic merit, professional qualifications, or legitimate educational objectives. This outcome would be particularly concerning for students who have already invested significant time and resources in their education based on the existing regulatory framework.

Fourth, more targeted alternatives could address fraud without disproportionately burdening legitimate participants.

I support stronger measures to prevent fraudulent employment arrangements and ensure that practical training remains directly related to students' academic fields. However, substantial fees imposed broadly on all participants are not necessarily an effective means of identifying or preventing fraud. I encourage DHS to consider alternative measures, including enhanced employer verification, risk-based compliance reviews, improved reporting mechanisms, and stronger enforcement against fraudulent institutions and employment arrangements. These approaches could strengthen program integrity while preserving legitimate educational and professional opportunities.

Furthermore, I urge DHS to carefully evaluate the broader economic and educational consequences of the proposed fee structure, including its effects on university enrollment, international student recruitment, employer participation, and the competitiveness of the American research and technology ecosystem.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee structure and preserve accessible practical training opportunities for qualified international students. At a minimum, DHS should conduct a more comprehensive assessment of the proposal's impact on current students, educational institutions, employers, and American technological competitiveness before adopting such substantial fees.

Maintaining a fair, predictable, and accessible practical training framework is essential to ensuring that the United States remains a leading destination for education, research, and innovation.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they impose disproportionate financial burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Michael VanJaarsveld
comments.commentText:
End the OPT Program immediately - it harms American youth and steals their opportunities.

I urge the Department of Homeland Security to end the Optional Practical Training program. The proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees are an acknowledgment that the current system is broken, but they are not enough. OPT is a government-created work authorization that places foreign students into American jobs and training opportunities at the direct expense of American youth. This is not a minor policy issue. It is a national emergency for the career futures of young Americans who did everything the system asked of them.

Recent data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York show unemployment among recent college graduates at approximately 5.2 percent and underemployment among employed recent graduates at 42.5 percent. These are Americans who studied, earned degrees, and took on student debt under the promise that education would open doors. Instead, many are sending out hundreds of resumes, facing rejection, or working in jobs that do not require their degrees. At the same time, hundreds of thousands of foreign students receive OPT work authorization each year and are placed into the same entry-level and early-career roles that American graduates need. Employers are not required to demonstrate that they first tried to hire qualified Americans. This is policy-driven displacement of American workers.

OPT functions as a theft of training and opportunity from American kids. It gives foreign students preferential access to practical experience, skill-building, and job networks in the United States without the caps, labor market tests, or recruitment protections that should apply when temporary foreign labor is authorized. STEM extensions make the problem worse by extending this advantage for years. The result is fewer first jobs, lower starting wages in some fields, and diminished career trajectories for American graduates. Allowing this to continue while young Americans struggle is indefensible.

The proposed fees correctly raise the cost of using OPT as a volume labor channel and should be finalized if the program is not immediately ended. But fees alone leave the structural preference in place. The only appropriate response is to terminate the program.

I therefore recommend that DHS:
- End the Optional Practical Training program as quickly as possible, with no new recommendations accepted after a short transition period.
- In the interim, finalize the $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees and impose a mandatory labor market test requiring documented good-faith recruitment of American applicants before any OPT hire.
- Immediately end the STEM OPT extension.
- Prioritize policies that expand training, apprenticeships, and entry-level opportunities for American citizens rather than foreign students.

American youth should not have their futures subordinated to a government program that hands their job and training opportunities to non-citizens. Ending OPT is the necessary step to protect their chance to build careers, support families, and pursue the American Dream. I urge the Department to act decisively in the national interest of American workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by CT State Community College
comments.commentText:
November 5, 2026

TO: Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs
Office of Management and Budget

Dear Desk Officer for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement,

We strongly oppose the proposed rule that will charge a $70,000 initial cost for Optional OPT and a $30,000 fee for subsequent applications. These exorbitant costs are unreasonable, detrimental to the economy, and not sufficiently supported by evidence. The new rule would practically eliminate most existing work authorization options for F1 visa international students and effectively dismantle a vital experiential learning pathway established by federal regulations. We, therefore, request that the administration withdraw the proposed rule.

The high fees would only differentiate students based on their financial resources. Empirical proof that these fees would be successful in reducing fraud should be provided by DHS.

Our institution is state funded and has no ability or room in the budget to afford this type of support for our F1 visa international students as it would cost between $1.4 and $1.75 million annually. Moreover, it would be impossible for us to implement a system to collect and pay the fee. Public higher education institutions operate under strict state fiscal controls and would face significant administrative and financial barriers in establishing such a payment mechanism. Moreover, since F1 visa international students represent only 1% of our total student population, we have a limited basis to advocate for the costs involved in setting up such a system, especially when doing so diverts critical state resources away from our core educational mission.

Although this proposed fee would be an extreme burden on higher educational institutions, the harm will be even greater for our students. $70,000 represents more than our students spend on their entire education (approximately $30-$45K). For a community college graduate, it most certainly represents more than they could possibly earn in the one year of work authorization that they are eligible for. Because of these factors, ALL of our students would lose out on an opportunity that they currently have the right to apply for. We average 25 students on Post-Completion OPT at any given time - a modest number in absolute terms, but one that represents individuals whose opportunities for clinical, technical, and applied training in the local community would be placed out of reach.

We understand that these rule changes have been proposed to “combat fraud.” However, the monies collected will not go to SEVP, DHS, or USCIS. Because of this, there is no way that the funds collected will do anything to offset or detect the alleged fraudulent behavior that the government describes. The high fees would only differentiate students based on their financial resources. Empirical proof that these fees would be successful in reducing fraud should be provided by DHS. Moreover, the diversion of these monies into the government’s general funds makes this proposal a tax, rather than a fee. As such, Congressional involvement is supposed to be required, raising serious concerns about the scope of executive agency authority. We wholeheartedly confirm that we are vigilant about fraud and ensure that students know how to follow the rules and comply with regulations.

Even though DHS projects the annual fee transfers to be in billions for this program, the net economic advantage is not the same as government revenue. The plan will cost American firms, discourage international enrollment, limit university research capacity, and encourage businesses to shift technical roles elsewhere. Our institution has benefited from international educational exchange, and we highly value the presence of international students on our campuses and in the United States. This proposed change, along with many other actions that the government has taken, will decimate international student and scholar enrollment in the US. Many students greatly appreciate having a short-term opportunity to implement the knowledge and skill sets that they gained during their degree programs, before returning to their home countries. When given a choice, future students will choose a country where they CAN get this opportunity, and where their cultural and economic contributions are welcomed rather than discouraged or threatened. Once this market share has been lost and the US relinquishes its reputation as a good place for quality higher education opportunities, the damage may be irreparable, ultimately undermining the international diversity and long-term competitiveness of American higher education.

For all of the above reasons, we urge DHS to revoke the proposed regulation.

Respectfully submitted,

International Student Admissions Team
CT State Community College
185 Main St., New Britain, CT 06085
CTState-InternationalAdmissions@ct.edu

DHS relies on its general power to set "conditions" of nonimmigrant admission, INA 214(a). In Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (Feb. 20, 2026), the Supreme Court held that a power to regulate does not include a power to tax. The charge is a tax under National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974): DHS admits it cannot keep the money, which goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts (31 U.S.C. 3302). The amount is tied to no cost of service, and its stated purpose is to deter OPT use. When Congress wanted an anti-fraud fee in INA 214, it enacted one expressly: $500 for certain H-1B and L petitions, earmarked for fraud detection (8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(12), 1356(v)). It has enacted no OPT charge. Washington Alliance v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), upheld OPT as a condition of status, not a power to raise revenue. With $109.4 billion in ten-year transfers, West Virginia v. EPA requires clear authorization, and Loper Bright gives DHS's reading no deference. On June 8, 2026, the District of Massachusetts vacated the $100,000 H-1B charge as an unlawful tax, and the First Circuit denied a stay on July 24, 2026.
II. ARBITRARY AND CAPRICIOUS: THE FEE DOES NOT FIT THE FRAUD
State Farm requires a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made. DHS's largest figure, 10,000 students at "suspect" employers, is about 3% of 2024 participants (194,554 OPT plus STEM OPT), and DHS does not say how many cases were confirmed. Every case DHS cites involves employers or document vendors, and every one was found with existing tools: prosecutions, SEVIS data, site visits. Yet the fee is charged to schools, often before any employer exists, since students may apply up to 90 days before completion without a job offer. A change of employer triggers no new fee. A fee that never sees the employer cannot deter employer fraud. DHS also charges $30,000 on STEM OPT, the track that already requires I-983 training plans, E-Verify and site visits. DHS rejected extending those safeguards without estimating their cost, and never considered employer attestation, registration or debarment, or its existing power to withdraw SEVP certification.
III. FLAWED ANALYSIS AND IGNORED RELIANCE
DHS projects $12.8 billion a year by applying the fees to historic participation, while conceding that schools will decline to pay. If the fee deters, the revenue figure is wrong. If the revenue materializes, the fee has not deterred. DHS quantifies no effects on enrollment, tax revenue or research staffing. Its wage evidence relies on 2001 data, and it admits it cannot quantify OPT's labor impact. It concedes schools may pass the cost to "all students," meaning American students. DHS v. Regents requires weighing reliance interests. DHS calls them "far outweighed" without measuring any. Students now enrolled chose schools and took on debt in reliance on OPT carrying no school charge, and in the transition year even students moving into STEM OPT would face $70,000. 1,389 of 2,478 affected schools (56%) are small entities, yet DHS did not consider tiered fees, caps, phase-ins or exempting pre-completion OPT (5 U.S.C. 603(c)).
IV. BROKEN BENCHMARK AND INADEQUATE PROCESS
DHS set $70,000 to be "comparable" to an H-1B charge that a court has since held unlawful. A single summer internship would trigger $70,000, and $100,000 with later OPT. DHS gave only 30 days to comment on the rule itself but 60 days on paperwork burden. Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 call for at least 60 days.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule, arguing it lacks statutory authority and is an arbitrary and capricious tax.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for later recommendations. Protecting U.S. workers and preventing fraud are legitimate goals, but DHS has not demonstrated that these fees would achieve either. The proposal would instead make access to practical training depend on wealth rather than merit or compliance.

First, the proposal assumes that reducing OPT participation would benefit American workers without establishing that outcome. A job no longer held by an OPT participant does not automatically become a job for a U.S. graduate. Employers might move work abroad, automate it, or leave positions vacant. DHS should substantiate its predictions with evidence of actual displacement and wage effects, rather than treating competition itself as proof of harm. If employers unlawfully exploit workers or violate hiring rules, enforcement should target those employers.

Second, a $70,000 payment does not verify that a student is qualified, a job is legitimate, or an employer complies with the law. A highly qualified student with a valid opportunity faces the same barrier as anyone else, while wealthy institutions can pay regardless of risk. If fraud is the concern, targeted audits, stronger reporting, and enforcement are more directly connected to that objective. DHS should explain why those alternatives are insufficient.

Third, complaints about tuition, scholarships, student debt, and university endowments do not establish a justification for OPT fees. International students are not universally scholarship recipients; aid comes from different funding sources and follows different eligibility rules. Endowments also vary widely and often contain restricted funds. Most importantly, the proposal does not guarantee that any fee revenue would lower tuition, repay federal loans, or fund U.S. students. College affordability deserves policies designed to address it directly.

Fourth, prospective application does not eliminate the harm to students already enrolled. Many chose U.S. universities and invested years of tuition and living expenses expecting that lawful, temporary training related to their degree would be a realistic option. A newly imposed institutional fee of this scale could make that option inaccessible even when the student meets every existing requirement. Smaller institutions and students without substantial financial resources would be especially disadvantaged.

Finally, DHS should account for costs beyond the number of OPT positions affected. International students contribute through tuition, housing, local spending, research, and work. Reduced enrollment and fewer graduates gaining experience here may harm universities, local economies, and employers. The relevant question is whether the claimed labor-market gains outweigh these losses, and DHS has not sufficiently established that they do.

American graduates deserve fair hiring, affordable education, and protection from exploitation. Those goals are not advanced simply by pricing international graduates out of lawful training. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and use proportionate, evidence-based oversight aimed at actual misconduct.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the high OPT fees and argues they create financial barriers without preventing fraud.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
Supplemental opposition comment: Further education should not reset the initial fee

I oppose the proposed OPT fee rule and request its withdrawal. This is an additional comment from the same commenter whose original submission has tracking number mvp-wb10-c5bl. It supplements that submission and should not be treated as the views of a separate person.

Sections V.A and VII.B.6 invite comment on an alternative under which the $70,000 initial fee could be required again when a student moves to a higher educational level. I specifically oppose that alternative. I understand that it is an option under consideration, rather than a description of the primary proposed fee schedule.

Completing a higher degree is not evidence of wrongdoing or a reason to presume that the student's next training opportunity imposes the same oversight burden as a first encounter with the program. A student may have an established record of lawful study and compliance. DHS should explain what additional administrative work or demonstrable risk would justify treating the next recommendation as a new $70,000 event instead of considering that existing record.

This alternative could also discourage educational progression. A university or potential employer deciding whether to support a graduate's training would have to consider another large payment. Students could face a financial penalty for investing in a master's or doctoral education, even where the later training develops substantially different skills. That would work against the educational purpose of practical training.

Before adopting any such reset, DHS should separately estimate its effects on progression between degree levels, participation in advanced training, and institutions' willingness to support graduates. The analysis should distinguish additional government processing costs from an intentional deterrent to participation and explain why less burdensome compliance measures would be insufficient.

DHS should withdraw the proposed rule and expressly reject the higher-degree reset alternative. My discussion of this alternative does not indicate support for the primary $70,000/$30,000 fee proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fee rule and requests its withdrawal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
Supplemental opposition comment: Disproportionate effects on small institutions

I oppose this proposed rule and request its withdrawal. This is a further submission by the same commenter associated with original tracking number mvp-wb10-c5bl, not an additional person's comment.

The small-entity analysis in section VII.B warrants much more attention. DHS estimates that 841 of the 1,389 small institutions examined, or 60.5 percent, would experience impacts exceeding one percent of estimated revenue. These are modeled estimates, not observed losses, but they underscore the scale of the proposal's potential consequences for institutions with limited resources.

Annual revenue alone does not measure the capacity to make a large payment for each student recommendation. DHS should examine unrestricted funds, operating margins, cash-flow timing, and the concentration of affected students within particular programs. Institutions with similar revenue can have very different financial obligations. A large upfront payment could lead a school to restrict recommendations, cut other services, or pass costs to students before any longer-term adjustment is possible.

Section VII.B.6 rejects a small-institution exemption in part because small entities account for a substantial share of regulated institutions and fraud could continue. The number of small institutions does not, by itself, establish their relative rate of noncompliance or demonstrate that a uniform fee is the best response. DHS should present evidence linking institution characteristics to actual oversight needs and evaluate targeted audits and enforcement using that evidence.

The alternatives analysis should also compare graduated charges, institutional caps, and other substantially less burdensome approaches, with transparent estimates of both compliance benefits and lost training opportunities. Any discussion of these alternatives is a request for a serious comparison, not an endorsement of a reduced version of this rule.

A fee that restricts access primarily according to an institution's financial resources does not necessarily improve compliance. DHS should withdraw the proposal and develop an evidence-based response to documented misconduct that does not impose disproportionate burdens on compliant small institutions and their students.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule, requesting its withdrawal due to negative impacts on small institutions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
Supplemental opposition comment: Financing arrangements and worker mobility

I oppose the proposed OPT fees and ask DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment supplements my original submission, tracking number mvp-wb10-c5bl, and represents the same commenter.

The proposal contemplates institutions shifting the financial burden to students or employers, even though the institution would make the required payment. DHS should analyze the consequences of those financing arrangements for students' ability to choose and leave an employer.

I recognize that section V.A states that changing employers would not itself trigger a new fee. That is a useful distinction, but it does not resolve the separate issue of who ultimately finances the existing fee. An employer willing to cover a large cost might seek repayment if a worker leaves, or seek to recover the payment through other compensation arrangements. I am identifying a foreseeable possibility that DHS should investigate, not claiming that such contracts are required by the proposal or describing any particular employer's conduct.

For a recent graduate with limited savings, a substantial repayment obligation could make it harder to leave unsuitable work, report mistreatment, or negotiate working conditions. Employers able to finance the fee could also gain a recruiting advantage unrelated to the educational quality of the training. Smaller employers and nonprofit organizations may be less able to participate even when they offer valuable supervised experience.

DHS should examine who would bear the costs under plausible financing arrangements, the likelihood and terms of repayment obligations, effects on compensation, and the consequences for mobility between employers. It should explain what safeguards would prevent the fee from undermining students' practical ability to exercise workplace rights. Simply observing that an employer change does not create another government fee is insufficient.

The proposal should be withdrawn. If DHS pursues further action, it should first assess these financing effects with evidence from students, institutions, and employers and compare targeted compliance measures that do not create a large financial dependency at the start of a training relationship.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and asks DHS to withdraw the rule due to financial burdens on students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
Supplemental opposition comment: Students should not lose opportunities because of institutional payment errors

I oppose the proposed rule and request its withdrawal. This is a supplemental comment by the same person who submitted original tracking number mvp-wb10-c5bl.

The payment sequence described in section V.A and the proposed regulatory amendments creates a serious implementation concern. The institution would have to pay before the designated school official recommends OPT, and the proposal would prevent approval where the required fee was not paid before the recommendation or was not paid at all.

The student does not control the institution's payment systems or the government's reconciliation of those payments. DHS should examine situations in which a school intends to comply but encounters a posting delay, a transaction-matching problem, or an inadvertent sequencing error. These are hypothetical implementation risks, not allegations about current systems. Nevertheless, the consequences could fall on a student who supplied accurate information and otherwise met the applicable requirements.

The rule should explain whether and how an institution could correct a premature recommendation or demonstrate a timely payment that was recorded incorrectly. DHS should specify notice procedures, an opportunity to cure clerical errors, responsibility for resolving payment discrepancies, and a meaningful process for correcting erroneous determinations. It should analyze how those procedures would interact with existing application and training timelines. Merely telling a student to start over may not preserve the original opportunity.

DHS should also estimate the cost of reconciling payment records with recommendations, training school staff, resolving exceptions, and assisting affected students. A system that appears administratively simple at the point of collection may impose substantial work on institutions and applicants.

My primary request is withdrawal of the fee proposal. If DHS nevertheless proceeds, it should not make an otherwise eligible student's training depend on an institutional accounting error that the student cannot prevent or promptly correct. Any further proposal should include explicit correction procedures and an assessment of these operational consequences before implementation.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and requests its withdrawal due to payment sequence concerns.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
Supplemental opposition comment: The participation scenarios do not establish a reliable expected outcome

I oppose the proposed rule and request its withdrawal. This submission supplements original tracking number mvp-wb10-c5bl and comes from the same commenter. It focuses specifically on the participation forecasts in sections VII.A.3.b and VII.A.4.a.

DHS acknowledges uncertainty about how participation would respond to the fees. Its high-participation scenario assumes no participation change and uses 2024 activity. The low-participation approach uses historical averages and assumptions about institutions financing initial OPT for students eligible for a STEM extension, including a historical continuation rate. The primary fee estimate then averages the high and low results.

These scenarios may illustrate possibilities, but their arithmetic average is not automatically a statistically supported expectation. DHS should explain why those endpoints are appropriate, what evidence supports their assumptions, and why they should receive equal weight. The difference between scenarios also involves different historical reference periods. That makes it harder to distinguish the estimated effect of the fee from differences in the underlying baseline.

A more informative analysis would hold the no-rule counterfactual constant and vary clearly identified behavioral assumptions. It should test participation responses across institutions with different financial resources, students with different access to funding, and employers with different capacities to finance training. It should also test reduced STEM participation rather than presuming STEM eligibility is sufficient to secure institutional financing. Historical continuation under the existing fee environment does not establish how students and institutions would behave after a large new charge.

DHS should publish enough detail to reproduce the forecasts and show how plausible alternative assumptions change the estimated number of lost training opportunities and the distribution of costs. Sensitivity analysis should be connected to evidence, rather than treating an average of selected scenarios as a substitute for evidence.

Because the participation forecast is central to evaluating this proposal, these uncertainties require a substantive response. DHS should withdraw the rule and undertake a more transparent, behaviorally grounded analysis before considering further action.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee rule.

OPT has long been an integral component of the F-1 student program, allowing international students to gain practical experience directly related to their fields of study. It serves important educational, economic, and workforce development purposes by connecting classroom learning with real-world training while helping U.S. employers recruit talent educated at American institutions.

The proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations would effectively eliminate access to OPT for many students and institutions. These amounts bear no apparent relationship to the actual cost of administering the program, maintaining SEVIS records, or investigating compliance concerns. Instead, they function as financial barriers designed to deter participation in an otherwise lawful program.

Research suggests that such fees could dramatically reduce OPT participation and international student enrollment. This would have serious consequences not only for international students but also for U.S. colleges, universities, employers, and local economies. International students contribute substantial tuition revenue that supports educational programs, research infrastructure, faculty positions, and opportunities for domestic students. A significant decline in enrollment would negatively affect these institutions and the communities they serve.

The proposal would also undermine the educational purpose of OPT. The fees would apply not only to post-graduation employment but also to pre-completion OPT used for internships and other short-term training experiences. As a result, a student seeking a brief internship could trigger a fee that far exceeds the value of the training opportunity itself. Faced with such costs, many schools would likely decline to recommend eligible students for OPT regardless of the educational merit of the experience.

The United States competes globally for talented students, researchers, and innovators. Other countries increasingly offer clear and accessible post-study work opportunities to attract highly skilled graduates. Restricting access to OPT through excessive fees would make U.S. institutions less competitive and encourage students to pursue education and careers elsewhere. This outcome would weaken, rather than strengthen, America's long-term economic and scientific leadership.

I am also concerned that DHS has not adequately demonstrated the legal or economic basis for the proposed fee amounts. The rule does not establish a clear connection between the fees and the government's actual costs of administering or enforcing the OPT program. Nor does it provide persuasive evidence that broad, punitive charges imposed on all institutions and students are a more effective solution than targeted compliance reviews, fraud investigations, and enforcement actions against specific bad actors.

Finally, the proposal contains significant ambiguities regarding when and how the $30,000 subsequent fee would apply. Such uncertainty makes it difficult for schools to evaluate potential liabilities and further undermines confidence in the proposal's economic analysis.

DHS already possesses substantial oversight tools through SEVIS, Designated School Official reporting requirements, STEM OPT training plans, employer attestations, compliance reviews, and investigations. If additional safeguards are needed, DHS should pursue targeted, evidence-based measures rather than imposing extraordinary fees that would effectively dismantle a longstanding educational training program.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and pursue alternative approaches that address compliance concerns while preserving the educational, economic, and workforce benefits of OPT.

Thank you for considering these comments.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule, arguing it imposes prohibitive financial barriers.

comments.commentText:
I am a US citizen, born and raised, who is currently enrolled in a PhD program in the US. The proposed rule introducing a $70,000 dollar fee for OPT for students on F-1 visas is frankly shortsighted and would be tantamount to shooting ourselves in the foot as a nation. The rule change appears to be intended to function as a deterrent against foreign students coming to the country and out competing domestic talent in the workforce. While this concern is understandable, this measure fails to address the core issues that face our educational institutions and the nation as a whole.

It goes without saying that a nation with the highest concentration of brilliant minds will be more competitive at a global scale than a nation of the same size with a lower concentration of equivalently capable workers. The US educational system should ideally work as a siphon, taking the most talented individuals from around the world and brings them to the US, ready to learn and ready to work, increasing our concentration of qualified workers while reducing the concentration of qualified workers in other countries. Giving our students the opportunity to surround themselves with the greatest minds from around the world, rather than just their immediate surroundings, is a part of what makes our educational system so strong. Removing the best minds from around the world would fundamentally damage our educational system.

Capability is not directly tied to the economic fortune of one's parents. At the age when most students are considering OPT, they have not had sufficient time to acquire capital of their own; rather any money they have is likely a reflection of their parents' wealth. The proposed rule change would destroy the value of a US education for most students who are worth teaching. There are plenty of wealthy foreigners who would love to send their unqualified and unruly children to the US to study at our institutions. However, these students are much less likely to recognize what a great opportunity an education in our country is, and will simply function as an anchor on our society before returning to their home countries to thrive on their parents wealth. The alternative would be foreign students taking out debts that they cannot pay back, then fleeing the country when the bill comes time to be paid. In both cases, they will have extracted value from the US without providing anything in return.

If the concern is that the number of foreign national students attending US institutions is too high, and too many people are coming to the US and out competing our own, the solution is not to place a fee on foreigners. The solution is to raise the academic bar for admission to US institutions as a foreign national so that we can be sure that we are getting only the best and brightest, perhaps placing a cap on the number of seats available at a given institution as a fraction of the student body. We should then provide this portion of students who are admitted to our institutions a clear path to citizenship, so that the effort spent on training them is not wasted by them leaving. This would ensure that we continue to reap the benefits of the US educational system without placing an anchor around our necks and without taking jobs away from qualified US born talent. A fee on entering the workforce would achieve the opposite effect.

As an employee at a higher ed institution, I strongly oppose this rule. The rule is ambiguous in both its scope and application. For instance, the proposed rule does not clarify whether the $70,000 fee is a one time, flat fee or whether it must be paid each time a student changes institutions. Moreover, the fee is directed to the Treasury rather than DHS, the department responsible for administering the OPT program. Fees are compulsory payments to offset an agency’s cost of providing a good or service. If the fee is not going to the agency providing the service, it cannot be considered a fee, but a tax. If enacted, this rule will disrupt research teams, employer partnerships, and workforce pipelines, and it would impact learning, mentorship, and career opportunities for both international and domestic students.

Crucially, the rule poses an existential threat to institutional financial stability at an exceptionally precarious moment. American higher education is currently navigating a severe "demographic cliff"—a sustained decline in the domestic college-aged population that has strained operating budgets nationwide. For years, international student enrollment has served as a critical counterweight to these domestic shortfalls. International students typically pay full non-resident tuition, providing essential revenue that supports departmental operations, student services, infrastructure, and institutional financial aid programs that directly benefit domestic students. Imposing a cost-prohibitive fee structure—whether passed on to students, shouldered by institutions, or transferred to employers—will inevitably divert international applications to competitor nations like China, European Union, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia. The resulting decline in international enrollment will decimate institutional tuition revenue at a time when colleges and universities can least absorb the blow. For many institutions already operating under razor-thin margins, this revenue shock will force severe budget cuts, the consolidation or elimination of degree programs, faculty layoffs, and diminished course offerings, ultimately hurting the entire academic community and American students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it.

1. The fee raises revenue and is not a real condition of admission (Sec. IV.C). DHS says the fees would go into the general Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302, and that ICE could not use them. DHS estimates annual collections of $8.4–16.5 billion. Yet it never ties the amounts to the cost of running OPT, and it does not rely on 31 U.S.C. 9701, which requires fees to reflect the cost or value of a service. A charge this large, unrelated to cost and paid into the general fund, works as a tax. INA 214(a)’s “time and conditions” authority does not clearly give DHS the power to raise billions in new revenue.

2. The fee does not target the fraud DHS describes (Sec. IV.A). DHS’s evidence is about shell employers, staged worksites, and sold offer letters. The fee, however, is paid by the school before the DSO recommendation. DHS admits the fee is not tied to any employer, and initial OPT does not require a job offer at all. Paying $70,000 tells a school nothing about whether a future employer is real. Bad actors can pass the cost on to students, while legitimate students at schools that cannot pay lose access. Because the money goes to the Treasury, the fee also does nothing about the problem DHS itself names: compliance resources have not kept pace with the program.

3. DHS rejected targeted alternatives for its own convenience. DHS considered applying the STEM OPT safeguards (training plans, employer site visits, reporting) to all OPT. It chose a fee instead mainly because a fee needs minimal government resources. Saving agency effort is not a reasoned basis for moving billions in costs onto schools and students. Checking employers addresses the fraud DHS describes. A per-student fee does not.

4. The fee amounts are arbitrary. DHS says it picked $70,000 to match the H-1B fee and to be “on par with” one or two years of tuition. Neither benchmark measures fraud risk, harm to the labor market, or administrative cost. The same $70,000 applies to a part-time pre-completion internship, which is the form of training closest to OPT’s educational purpose. DHS itself expects pre-completion OPT to decline.

5. DHS quantifies the costs but not the benefits (Sec. VII.A). DHS estimates annualized costs of up to $8.2 billion (primary estimate $4.1 billion) and transfers of $12.8 billion per year. It gives no estimate of fraud prevented or U.S. jobs gained. It uses unpaid fees as a stand-in for lost value and does not estimate lost tuition, tax revenue, research output, or enrollment. Executive Order 12866 requires a reasoned finding that benefits justify costs, and this record cannot support one.

6. Small institutions are hit hardest (Sec. VII.B). By DHS’s own estimate, 841 of 1,389 small affected institutions would face transition-year costs above 1% of revenue, and 116 would face costs above 20%. DHS rejected a small-entity exemption because small entities make up 56% of regulated schools. That is exactly why the Regulatory Flexibility Act requires DHS to reduce the burden on them, not a reason to skip it.

7. DHS dismisses reliance interests and rushes the process (Sec. VI). Current students chose their programs, took on debt, and planned careers under the existing rules, and the fee would apply to them partway through their degrees. DHS also says schools may pass the cost to all students, which means U.S. students could end up paying for it. A rule with this much economic impact deserves the 60-day comment period that E.O. 12866 calls for, not 30 days.

8. The rule turns OPT into a privilege of wealth. Well-endowed schools and wealthy families can pay. Strong students at public, regional, and community institutions often cannot. The rule selects students by ability to pay, not by merit or integrity.

Recommendation: Withdraw the rule. To address fraud, DHS should pursue employer verification, more site visits, and enforcement against identified shell employers, and it should seek appropriations or a cost-based fee to fund SEVP oversight.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposed OPT fees appear to assume that reducing access to employment for international graduates will benefit American workers. However, this assumption overlooks how hiring decisions actually work.

Employment opportunities are not automatically transferred from one group of candidates to another. Employers hire based on qualifications, business needs, available budgets, and the expected value of a position. If an additional $70,000 fee makes hiring an international graduate financially impractical, the employer is not necessarily going to hire an American candidate instead.

In many cases, the position may simply remain unfilled. A company may cancel a planned hire, reduce its research activities, delay product development, or decide that a project is no longer financially viable. For startups and small businesses, one additional expense of this size can fundamentally change whether a hiring decision makes economic sense.

This distinction is important. A reduction in international hiring does not necessarily represent an increase in domestic employment. It could instead mean fewer jobs overall, less business investment, and reduced economic activity. American workers may ultimately lose opportunities when companies scale back or move their operations to other countries.

The proposed fee structure also raises questions about fairness and proportionality. It applies a substantial financial burden regardless of the size of the employer, the salary associated with the position, the nature of the work, or the actual risk of fraud. A small research organization and a large multinational corporation face the same fee, despite having very different financial capacities.

If the objective is to prevent fraudulent employment and protect U.S. workers, enforcement should focus on employers and arrangements that violate the rules. Stronger verification, targeted audits, and meaningful penalties for confirmed violations would address these concerns more directly.

Before adopting such a significant financial barrier, DHS should provide convincing evidence that it will actually improve employment outcomes for American workers rather than simply reduce legitimate hiring and economic activity.

I urge DHS to reconsider the proposal and evaluate its effects on total employment, business investment, and the competitiveness of American companies, not merely the number of international graduates participating in OPT.

A sudden introduction of fees as high as $70,000 for initial OPT participation and $30,000 for subsequent participation could disrupt these established plans. Universities may have already admitted students, committed research funding, and allocated resources based on existing program rules. Employers may have developed hiring plans around anticipated graduate availability.

If the financial conditions of OPT change dramatically, these institutions may face unexpected costs and difficult decisions. Even the uncertainty surrounding future participation could make universities and employers more hesitant to invest in international talent.

There is also a broader issue of international confidence. The United States competes globally for students, researchers, and highly skilled professionals. Predictable policies are an important part of that competition. When the rules governing post-graduation opportunities become financially uncertain, prospective students may reasonably consider countries where the transition from education to employment is more predictable.

This could have consequences beyond immediate OPT participation, affecting future university enrollment, research collaborations, and the willingness of international talent to build professional connections in the United States.

DHS should explain how institutions and individuals who have already made substantial commitments under the existing framework will be protected from unexpected financial and operational disruptions. Any significant policy change should include a careful assessment of reliance interests, reasonable transition arrangements, and sufficient advance notice.

Immigration policy should be enforceable, but it should also be predictable. Long-term educational, research, and business decisions require a stable regulatory environment.

Fees are compulsory payments to offset an agency’s cost of providing a good or service. If the fee is not going to the agency providing the service, it cannot be considered a fee, but a tax. Imagine an international graduate student who conducts research at a top US university funded by federal research grants. This student will now be forced to immediately return to their home country instead of giving back the US their expertise that our federal funding dollars paid for during their graduate schooling.

The rule also also raises the bugaboos of "fraud" and "abuse" --- problems that do not exist in reality. The proposed rule text claims this rule will impose "fees to combat fraud and abuse, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers". It will do the opposite. It will weaken US research & development across academia and industry. Schools across US already have a robust system of oversight through the designated school officials for vetting OPT applications and prevent fraud.

Ultimately, the proposed fee is a financial barrier to participation in the OPT program, potentially discouraging international students from studying in the US. If enacted, this rule will disrupt research teams, employer partnerships, and workforce pipelines, and it would impact learning, mentorship, and career opportunities for both international and domestic students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose and request the withdrawal of the proposed OPT fees. Fraud prevention is legitimate; financial exclusion is not evidence-based enforcement. The rule risks being "arbitrary, capricious" and "in excess of statutory ... authority" under 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A), (C).

WHERE IS THE SPECIFIC FEE AUTHORITY? DHS invokes general immigration and admission authority (8 U.S.C. 1103(a), 1184(a)), neither of which expressly authorizes these charges. Congress separately provided a student-monitoring fee based on "cost per alien" (8 U.S.C. 1372(e)(4)(A)). Under 31 U.S.C. 9701(b), government service charges must be "fair" and consider government costs and recipient value. In National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336, 341 (1974), the Court observed: "A 'fee' connotes a 'benefit'." DHS must explain why these deterrent charges are authorized fees, not exclusionary assessments. Under Loper Bright v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 412 (2024), "courts must exercise their independent judgment" on statutory authority.

DHS ADMITS THE MONEY WILL NOT FUND ICE OVERSIGHT. The notice says "ICE would not maintain or use the funding" (91 FR 64576, IV.C): revenue goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. The deposit statute (31 U.S.C. 3302(b)) does not authorize imposing the fee. How do these payments remedy enforcement shortfalls? Reducing the number of lawful participants is not equivalent to identifying fraud. DHS must prove how these amounts prevent fraud, not merely exclude poorer applicants.

PAYMENT CANNOT VERIFY A JOB THAT DOES NOT YET EXIST. DHS admits a student "does not have to secure a training opportunity" before a school recommendation (91 FR 64569, III.D.1). How can advance payment verify an employer or worksite that may not exist yet? Wealthy bad actors can pay; compliant students may not. Wealth is not proof of compliance. DHS must publish confirmed fraud rates, denominators, and outcomes, not generalize from anecdotes.

THE ECONOMIC ANALYSIS IS CIRCULAR. DHS projects roughly $12.8 billion in annualized transfers and $4.1 billion in annualized costs (primary estimates, 3% discount; 91 FR 64579, VII.A.1). It says it "uses unpaid OPT fees as a proxy" for lost OPT opportunities (91 FR 64588, VII.A.5.b). An agency-set fee cannot establish the value of lost wages, training, research, or enrollment. DHS also projects transition-year impacts exceeding 20% of revenue for 116 small institutions (91 FR 64595, VII.B.4). The rule does not quantify net U.S.-worker job or wage gains.

RELIANCE INTERESTS CANNOT BE DISMISSED BY A 60-DAY DELAY. Students committed years and substantial tuition to U.S. degrees under an established OPT system. The proposal could charge $70,000 even for an initial post-effective-date STEM extension where earlier OPT required no such fee. DHS must assess these commitments, not merely dismiss them. In DHS v. Regents, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), DHS was "required to assess whether there were reliance interests" (slip op. 26).

DHS REJECTS BETTER-TARGETED MEASURES WITHOUT COMPARABLE PROOF. Employer verification, risk-based site inspections, payroll audits, data-matching, penalties for sham employers, and stronger DSO accountability directly address the cited abuses. DHS dismisses these approaches without showing fees work better. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983), requires the agency to "examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation." These fees treat lawful students as risks to be priced out.

Please withdraw the proposal. Alternatively, disclose precise authority, fee calculations, fraud data, economic/reliance analysis, and comparisons with targeted enforcement; reopen comments. Wealth is not compliance, and price is not proof.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they are financially exclusionary and lack statutory authority.
